The Galerie du Bolero in Versoix Switzerland presents the exhibition Cités Délaissées by Jean-Marc Yersin; Les carnets d’un autre temps No. 5 is the accompanying publication. Jean-Marc Yersin writes:

In 2016, an old childhood friend, settled in Gary Indiana, south of Chicago, invited me to explore his city, hit hard by the crisis. During that trip, I used a sketchbook to build coherence into the series and lay the first groundwork for a future publication, Crise, which naturally became the first volume of the Carnets d’un autre temps.

In the early 1990s, I found myself, for several months, drawn along the same long highway route, tirelessly casting the gaze of a captive spectator over a landscape from which rose a succession of structures, either bursting up from the ground or cutting into the scenery. Driving at daybreak along still-deserted roads, I contemplated these constructions like a traveler discovering the vestiges of a lost civilization, struggling to grasp their original purpose.

In their own way, these monuments spoke eloquently of the brutality of our relationship with our environment. We were still far from grasping the risk of our civilization’s collapse, and yet I found myself wondering how our infrastructure might one day be seen by others, in another time.

From that questioning was born the desire to draw up a kind of photographic inventory of these places in transition, taking care to detach them as far as possible from any temporal anchor so that they might escape their role, their function, and appear instead as newly unearthed monuments.

Though drawn from the most varied locations, the resulting images come together to form a kind of archaeological catalogue of a future time or an imaginary atlas of a territory yet to come which I published in the Carnets d’un autre temps collection.

So many habits, customs, and even everyday workings and exchanges had been dematerialized by the digital revolution that cities had lost their very reason for being. They were no longer the places one needed to be; there was no need to live there one could work from elsewhere, from other horizons. Already, in the time of pandemics, then during the war, or amid the floods, those who had houses beyond the city walls had been quick to flee the cities.

Since then, everyone came to spend more and more time in this new virtual world, a kind of Meta-City of every possibility, where everything seemed simpler, more seductive, and immediately accessible. There, one encountered flawless, faultless avatars, satisfying our every whim, lulled by an illusion of immortality. Stripped of their appeal, the cities could no longer seduce. Falling birth rates had emptied them, and life there had become so difficult, with shortages so frequent and the climate so stifling.

Curiously, these Cités délaissées (Neglected Cities), frozen in a remarkable state of preservation, would not be in ruins as though their last inhabitants had shielded them from the ravages of time… but the reality was darker: they had not imagined that one day, behind these elegant glass façades, they themselves would be replaced by artificial intelligences of absolute docility, working around the clock for the sole cost of the energy consumed… With no further need for humans, these intelligences organized the upkeep of the abandoned cities themselves… a kind of illusion of an urban civilization, grown virtual within a lifeless setting…

Jean-Marc Yersin

…Our modernity isn’t a cheerful one, but your images are radical… – Peter Knapp

At first glance, Jean-Marc Yersin’s photographs seem to echo the idea of “non-places” developed by anthropologist Marc Augé in his 1992 book:

“Yet non-places are the measure of our age a measure that is quantifiable, and that could be taken by adding together, with a few conversions between surface area, volume, and distance, the air, rail, and motorway routes and the mobile capsules known as ‘means of transport’ (planes, trains, coaches), the airports, railway stations, and spaceports, the great hotel chains, the leisure parks, and the big retail centers, and finally the intricate web of wired or wireless networks that draw on outer space itself for a form of communication so strange that it often puts the individual in touch with nothing more than another image of himself.”

And yet, across the Carnets d’un autre temps (Vestiges, Crise, La Ligne), it is clearly the temporal dimension that above all shapes the perception of these spaces. Snapshots give way to what might be called ‘time-shots,’ which give free rein to the cold, structured melancholy emanating from these derelict industrial structures. The black and white contributes to smoothing the spaces and recording the marks of aging on materials and equipment, in a spirit that recalls both the so-called ‘documentary’ photography of the Farm Security Administration, set up during the Great Depression by Franklin Roosevelt in 1937, and the practices of the Düsseldorf School, following the work and teaching of Bernd and Hilla Becher. But Jean-Marc Yersin adopts neither the social dimension of the American model nor the systematic character of the German school. His model is that of a tourist, the contemporary flâneur who wanders through chosen landscapes that seem suspended between their industrious past life and their future ruin. In short, his photographs display an overabundance of emptiness, and the unusual solitude of these finite spaces (to paraphrase and invert Blaise Pascal’s famous reflection — ‘The eternal silence of these infinite spaces frightens me’) it is not tragic. It invites the viewer to seek out the traces or marks writing, graffiti, signals of a human presence that seems to haunt these no man’s lands.

Cités délaissées shifts into uchronia (or ‘alternate history’) and dystopia, a genre especially prized in science-fiction literature and film (1984, La Jetée, Stalker, Planet of the Apes, THX 1138, 12 Monkeys, Blade Runner, Terminator, Dark City, Oblivion, Elysium, I, Robot, I Am Legend, Interstellar, Ready Player One, etc.). One also thinks of the comic-book series conceived by François Schuiten and Benoît Peeters since 1983: The Obscure Cities (Les Cités obscures). The fable Jean-Marc Yersin imagines makes use of photography, which has a reputation for being the trace of a past moment. Here, it is the present of the public architecture we know that is conjugated in the future tense or rather, the future perfect. This very particular tense in the French language expresses the past of the simple future (here: once climate change will have made cities uninhabitable, life will be replaced by artificial intelligences). It is a form of anticipation whose use extends to the formulation of hypotheses or outcomes (humans will have been replaced). And it is by way of fiction that Cités délaissées meets Marc Augé’s thinking: these photographic architectures give us another image of ourselves, in absentia.

Philippe KaenelAssociate Professor of Contemporary Art History at the University of Lausanne.

BiographyAfter training in an advertising photography studio in Geneva, Jean-Marc Yersin practiced his craft across a wide range of fields. During a long trip through North America in 1981, he created Downtown, questioning the place of the individual in the American city.

Together with his wife, archaeologist Pascale Bonnard Yersin, he took over the direction of the Swiss Camera Museum in Vevey in 1991, and the couple were among the founders of the Festival Images’95, whose foundation he chaired until 2000. Once the Museum’s full extension and renovation was completed in 2012, Jean-Marc Yersin was gradually able to return to his own photographic projects, to which he has devoted himself more freely since his retirement in 2018.

Through his photographs, he questions how what may well become our future ruins might one day be seen by others, in another time. From that questioning was born the desire to draw up a kind of atlas of these places in transition, which he publishes under the title Les carnets d’un autre temps, of which four volumes have already appeared. These publications have also been the subject of various exhibitions and screenings, both in Switzerland and in France.

In his practice, Jean-Marc Yersin conceives and produces the entirety of his projects himself, placing great importance on the physical materiality of his prints as well as on the layout of his publications and the hanging of his exhibitions. Inspired by the kinship that inkjet printing has renewed with the world of engraving, he has equipped himself with his own print studio, where he has developed his own style of black-and-white prints using very deep inking, even for large formats prints.

One day in June 2024, having just finished a few darkroom tests as part of my research into natural alternative developers this time formulated with chicory I sent my results and my new recipe sheet to Gilles Decamps, our editor-in-chief at The Eye of Photography.

Among the black-and-white images I had taken in the field, I sent him some poppies that had caught my eye.

During our phone call, Gilles told me that poppies were the favorite flower of Jean-Jacques Naudet, Founder and Director of this online publication. I listened to Gilles and made a note of it.

For some years now, I too have been drawn to these flowers, which paint such beautiful palettes of color across our fields and those of my village in Burgundy and I love photographing them.

From Claude Monet, one of whose works, completed in 1873, Les coquelicots is among the most famous, alongside champ de coquelicots from 1889 by Vincent Van Gogh, and also the work of great photographers such as Denis Brihat, who captured the coquelicot volant in his study series on this flower how could one not love a poppy, this flower so light that, as you pass close by and pause to look, it seems to greet you with its red cheeks, its petals fluttering in the wind, as if to say hello and goodbye?

So today, I have decided to take the step and offer you a few of these images of bright red poppies, a symbol of honor and remembrance flowers that do not fear drought, and which, since yesterday, have begun appearing again in our fields and in the places where we live. A plant they say, to calm and ease stress.

With Jean-Jacques Naudet and his family in mind, here are a few photographs taken over the past several years.

A humble tribute to this warm-hearted man, who devoted his whole life to revealing facets of the world of Photography to us, to passing them on, and to making us want to better know those who, for years, have been passionate about the eighth art for both analog and digital works.

Jacques Revon

Image 61: Portfolio : “This book was created during a period of returning home—both physically and emotionally. The desire to capture ephemeral forms of social reality underlies all of Brassaï best work of the 1930s – both the photographs of graffiti and the images of Parisian nights and their “secrets” and reflects the particular cultural climate of the late 20s and 30s in which the emergent science of ethnography had much in common with the Surrealist avant-garde.– Marja Warehime, Brassaï: Images of Culture and the Secret Surrealist Observer

Those eyes. We must talk about those tremendously absorbing eyes that were so large and engrossing that he always emphasised his peepers in the self-portraits that he painted or just simply sketched. When the Transylvanian-born Brassaï was bestowed the Ordre des Arts et des Lettres by the French Ministry of Culture in 1974, an award that he indeed was very proud of (though he detested the ceremonial formalities), he tainted the calligraphical handwriting on the diploma with his own scribbles which he found to be a necessary addendum: “Otherwise known as Dracula.”

Anaïs Nin observed how totally hypnotised Brassaï looked every time those eyes caught anything that enticed him. And Henry Miller who earnestly claimed that Brassaï’s rarest gift as a photographer was his normal vision described how apt his friend was “to meet in the most unexpected quarters. He was always on the qui vive [lookout], always sniffing the air, always poking in corners, always looking beyond you. Everything, literally, was of interest to him.” Those eyes were like the eyes of Ana Torrent in Victor Erice’s The Spirit of the Beehive (1973) or even more so in Carlos Saura’s Cría cuervos (1976), eyes that took in everything and made an indelible universe out of it.

Brassaï was of course also a writer (he authored several books including a novel) and more so a voracious reader who left many of his favourite books overflowing with comments. One such work was Henri Poincaré’s Science and Hypothesis (1902) in which he had underlined the French mathematician’s sentence “It is always with our senses that we serve our instruments.” Brassaï argued that “The photograph is the daughter of the world of externals, of the living second and as such will always keep something of the historic or scientific about it; but it is also the child of the rectangle, a child of the beaux-arts which requires one to fill up the space agreeably or harmoniously.”

A very fine clue as to what Brassaï was looking for in his photography comes from his description of an artist from another medium: “[Pierre Reverdy’s poems] were clear, strong, and pure as crystal. Each line was like a snapshot of an object or event, caught on the wing, firmly secured yet alive with their original power, captured forever. I was amazed by this great poet’s gift for giving a permanent form to things which had struck him, and by the sharpness of his vision. And how fastidiously he eradicated all signs of sentiment or sentimentality from his poems, taking care to conceal anything of himself behind other things.”

As geniuses have their own way of facing up to things, the story (true or false) goes that one night towards the end of 1929, Brassaï who so far had regarded photography with reluctancy and hardly as a mode of artistic expression was on the Pont Neuf with André Kertész when his Hungarian compatriot made him realise that capturing the beauty of Paris during the hours of darkness was by and large a conceivable thing with a camera. Within the next few years Brassaï created his most fantastic series of images that came out in December 1932 as Paris de nuit, one of the most famous and special photobooks of all time.

“A creative person is finally born when he has found his own route and voice. The only birthdate which matters to me is not Brassó 1899, but Paris 1933,” explained Brassaï who took as nom de guerre the name of his birthplace about this overdetermined change of heart regarding photography.

He once drew a parallel to a story that Isadora Duncan had told him many years ago when her fabulously wealthy lover Paris Eugène Singer engaged a consummate pianist for her whose face, however, she detested so much that he was required to play behind a screen during her dance practices. In due course Duncan and the pianist had to travel together in an equipage, alone. “The carriage came to an abrupt stop and she was catapulted into his arms. She said to me, ‘I stayed there; I understood it was to be the greatest love of my life.’”

Brassaï’s friend David Travis, who ran the Department of Photography at the Art Institute of Chicago for a quarter of a century, observes in his book At the Edge of the Light: Thoughts on Photography and Photographers, Talent and Genius that only a small number of the practitioners who created the golden era of photography in Paris were French, and what distinguished Brassaï “is that he wanted to picture what was obscured from the everyday view, what was dangerous, and, most of all, what was forbidden”. What made his work unusually perilous was his bulky camera gear which often put him in harm’s way a bellowed Voigtländer that took 6.5 x 9 cm glass plates, a tripod and explosively loud magnesium flash powder charges.

Brassaï’s nephew Philippe Ribeyrolles, who supervises the Estate Brassaï Succession, delineates in Brassaï: The Eye of Paris what a remarkably distinctive being his uncle was, and how much he loved to visit Brassaï and his wife’s little apartment at 81 rue du Faubourg Saint-Jacques “which had been turned into a fascinating Wunderkammer”: “His lively expression would make the rounds of the room and then, through the pronounced sphericality of his eyes, he would turn and suddenly stare at me with disarming intensity. He had quite an effect on me but, most of all, he was spellbinding!”

Ribeyrolles’s words above come from the very fine catalogue that sided a couple of exhibitions in Italy a few years ago, and which luckily inspired Moderna Museet in Stockholm to now present Brassaï: The Secret Signs of Paris. Whereas the Moderna catalogue is quite meh, the reproductions are flat and so are the essays, the exhibition right here (with its dark nooks and cubbyholes) is what happens when you win in life.

What gathers under the “secret signs” designation are Brassaï’s photographic project of graffitied wall figures and his masterpieces from nighttime Paris of the early 1930s, replete with the nocturnal creatures who not only made the city a dangerous place but all the more gorgeous and alive. All these stunning prints (often 17 x 23 cm in size) on glazed photo paper are done by the master himself, and they do have an aura. In the lovelessness of this day and age it is nice to hear the sound of mandolins for once.

Marcel Proust was Brassaï’s literary hero (his book on Proust was published posthumously) and Brassaï explained how “Photography illuminated for me a new Proust, as a kind of photographer of mental images, with his own being as the sensitised plate; he was able to capture and store thousands of impressions during his childhood, and when he set off in search of lost time, he constantly developed and fixed them, so that the latent image of his whole life was made visible as the gigantic photograph which is Remembrance of Things Past [1913–27].”

There is no doubt that Brassaï’s photosensitive plate during the 1930s was a very personalised form of primal therapy in which he captured the untamed energy of the city through the unique probity and scotopic vision. with which he originated these images where lust joins hands with love, misconduct with merriment and darkness with light. There is not a photograph by Brassaï that is existentially pitchy (nor straight-up uncomplicated for that matter). Behold his quarrelling couple from a bar in Montparnasse, the tough guy apache with his thick cap and the beautiful girl with her hallmark kiss curl, inseparable by Brassaï’s silver lining.

“Brassaï does not wait for the curtain to raise; he waits for it to fall,” suggested Henry Miller in his essay on Brassaï, “The Eye of Paris” (1933). And obviously, Brassaï’s nights were much in contrast to the constant sundowns of Travis Bickle in Scorsese’s 1976 film Taxi Driver: “All the animals come out at night – whores, skunk pussies, buggers, queens, fairies, dopers, junkies … sick, venal. Someday a real rain will come and wash all this scum off the streets.”

Nighttime Paris for Brassaï meant unadulterated intoxication, the joy of holding on to life and a romance for the people he encountered. The streetwalker Georgette in Philippe Soupault’s novel Last Nights of Paris (1928) was one of them: “Thanks to her the Parisian night became an unknown domain, an immense land of wonders full of flowers, birds, glances and stars, a hope thrown out into space.”

Brassaï, the beholder of “man’s strange customs”, expressed that “Night does not show things, it suggests them. It disturbs and surprises us with its strangeness. It liberates forces within us which are dominated by our reason during the daytime.”

In his photobook The Secret Paris of the 30s, which had to wait until 1976 to get published, Brassaï writes that “Just as night birds and nocturnal animals bring a forest to life when its daytime fauna falls silent to the ground, so night in a large city brings out of its den an entire population that lives its life completely under cover of darkness […] Rightly or wrongly, I felt at the time that this underground world represented Paris at its least cosmopolitan, at its most alive, its most authentic.”

In the earliest photographs that he took for Paris de nuit, these nocturnal animals were more like extras as if brought there by forces of lyrical necessitarianism in stage sceneries full of atmospheric textures and a chiaroscuro never before seen in photography or anywhere else. The more confident Brassaï became with his camera work, the more he dared to let these captivating figures populate the screen as full characters. It is interesting to note that Paris de nuit was the original seed for the French filmmakers of poetic realism who treated their underworld subjects (naughty or nice) without scorn, disregard or sensationalism.

Brassaï took so many pictures during these night ramblings with the tripoded Voigtländer, and his bag loaded with twenty-four glass plates, that they could have filled up several photobooks. In 1932 he was notified by a friend that publisher Charles Peignot of Arts et Métiers graphiques was on the hunt for a photographer for a book about Paris after dark, which was what evolved into Paris de nuit.

While Brassaï’s sixty-four photogravure-printed images in the spiralbound book became an instantaneous success, critically as well as commercially, much of the experience proved a great disappointment for the author: the publisher fouled up the credits on the cover so that the essayist became the star of the book, and on top of it all the negatives disappeared for fifty years after the book was launched in English too, along with an exhibition in London’s Mayfair in late 1933 (an exhibition that totally changed the course of Bill Brandt’s photography). There was also another book, published outside of Brassaï’s control, that made every effort to turn his meticulous photography into a prurient sleaze show.

After four years in Berlin in the early 1920s, with art studies, get-togethers with the leading poets, and a rather haphazard journalistic career among a lot of the new illustrated magazines of the era during which he evolved the knack of using different personas as a working method (“every person I meet knows a different mask”), something that he later used elaborately as Brassaï, the Photographer he made the French capital a permanent home.

As Marja Warehime notes in Brassaï: Images of Culture and the Secret Surrealist Observer, “The twenty-four-year-old Gyula Halász who got off the train at the Gare de l’Est in February, 1924, and grabbed a taxi for rue Delambre [where his long-term-stay hotel was located between the lively boulevard du Montparnasse and the Cimetière du Montparnasse where he was put to rest in 1984] hardly expected to become Brassaï, one of the most important figures in European photography.” In an early letter to his mother and father, he penned: “I’ve become interested, more than anything else, in the way Paris lives and moves and how one moves with it.”

One day in 1925 when Brassaï was visiting his friend Léopold Zborowski, a Polish poet who tried to make some sort of a career in Paris as an art dealer, someone rang on the door to the flat on rue Joseph Bara. It was the incomparable Atget, with a portfolio of large prints (as large as his plates) that overwhelmed the not-yet Brassaï: “Streets and alleyways of the Paris quartiers, the façades of buildings, dark courtyards with their little boxes for the concierge, costermongers, brothels, street girls, ancient signs, small-time street traders all redolent of Paris and its atmosphere. They were everyday photographs but they had meaning and an expression of extraordinary beauty.”

As a child Brassaï had spent a whole and very joyous year in Paris in the early 1900s together with his erudite father, a dedicated Francophile and a university professor back in Hungary. Once Brassaï left his youthful art studies in Budapest in 1921, he never again returned to his precious motherland nor the Alps of his youth. In a letter to a friend in 1976 he confided that “I still cling to a nostalgia for the fir trees, the larches, the rhododendrons, the gentian. It is my only Heimweh [homesickness].” But Paris was his steadfast place in the world, and few of course have shaped that world as quintessentially as Brassaï.

He established this habit early on of rolling out of bed at sundown for another daily dose of uninhibited wandering feats between Montparnasse and Montmartre: “At that time Montparnasse was like a powerful drug; we were a large group of friends, which included the poet Henri Michaux, and we stayed at Le Dôme until one in the morning, only to move to La Coupole, which closed an hour later. When time was up there, we migrated to Aux Îles Marquises in the rue de la Gaîté, always ending up at the Gare Montparnasse, when it was time for fresh coffee and the newspapers.”

In his foreword to Letters to My Parents (published in 1978), Brassaï explains that since that precise moment when he understood “that the camera was capable of capturing the beauty of the Parisian night (the beauty with which I had fallen passionately in love with during my bohemian adventures), I pursued photography solely for my own enjoyment. At the same time, I also understood that for an artist to chose the form of expression was not irrelevant in a given era.” The first thing that he did with his new Voigtländer camera was to walk around the Jardin du Luxembourg to take his earliest pictures as Brassaï. That marvellous garden was the first love of his life when he was five.

In Berlin he had devoured Oswald Spengler’s two-volume work The Decline of the West (1918/22) and recognised the polymath’s standpoint that “the artist’s place had been usurped by the engineer and the builder”. Yet nothing would diminish Brassaï’s personal creative yearnings as he was on the hunt for something relevant for his time: “I hardly need to add that early in my stay I was so enthralled by the richness of Parisian life that I wasn’t inclined to confine myself to the four walls of an atelier all alone. Life seemed much more exciting than the arts,” he wrote.

The proud urbanite’s flâneurial search for modernity was put into words early on in Baudelaire’s patchy Paris Spleen (1855–67): “The solitary meditative walker draws an unusual excitement from this universal communion. The man who easily joins with the crowd knows feverish pleasures, of which the egotist, closed like a chest, and the lazy person, imprisoned like a mollusc, will forever be deprived. He adopts all professions as his own, all the joys and woes which circumstance presents to him.”

A major proportion of The Secret Signs of Paris exhibition at the Moderna Museet in Stockholm is fixed on a series that Brassaï initiated in 1932 significantly the year when he and Picasso met and became friends for life a series that he worked on for nearly twenty years, and with the additional intention to register how these primordial images (or indeed signs) changed over time in their rough urban element. “Photography was, in Brassaï’s view, a means of exposing what was fundamental in human activity,” writes Alain Sayag in Brassaï: The Monograph. “That in turn led him to take interest in an ephemeral and underrated form of expression that went back to the earliest days of mankind: graffiti.”

The Stockholm catalogue has an essay by Brassaï (written in 1958 after these pictures had been on show at the MoMA, an exhibition organised by Edward Steichen) titled “Parisian Graffiti”, in which he suggests that a city wall is like a fishing net that accumulates the old archetypes from the metaphorical depths of human waters, and that the wall tantalises “the ‘unsophisticated’, the ill-adapted, the disinherited, the frustrated, and the rebellious (revolutions always start out on a wall) indeed all those who have something with which to reproach society or existence in general. For a wall exorcises.”

The carnality of this series, that was illuminated in Brassaï’s book Graffiti, published in 1960, is left out at the Moderna but you still get the excess humour, sensuality and the mystique from what he photographed in the working-class areas of Paris and which you still for that matter, in the same manner, can discover in the backstreets of Pompeii. (The most significant sort of graffiti that has taken over Paris today is the artist Invader’s mosaic squares, depicting those sweet and pixellated Space Invaders above 1,500 street corners around the city.)

Elliott Erwitt claimed that photography was about “finding something interesting in an ordinary place. I’ve found it has little to do with the things you see and everything to do with the way you see them.” The way that Brassaï observed things both in what would eventually become Paris de nuit and through his perception of graffiti was a port of entry to the influential art journal Minotaure and its dozen issues between 1933 and the outbreak of WWII, but also proved a fast lane into the daggered hearts of the surrealists.

As everyone could notice who were lucky enough to experience the nonpareil Surréalisme centennial at the Centre Pompidou (just before Beaubourg closed its doors in 2025 for renovations), the greatest pieces of Surrealism were often made outside of the dictates of André Breton. “Nothing is finer or greater than reality itself; why wrap it up in our own confused emotions?” asked Brassaï in 1932. “Just as a poet reclaims overused words, the creator of images also challenges everything that has become too familiar. He wants to restore the power of the ordinary, disregarded things, to surprise us with what we are tired of seeing every day, or which through habit we no longer even notice.”

The British surrealist and printmaker Stanley Hayter, who established the famous Atelier 17 in Montparnasse, acknowledged Brassaï’s “enormous human appreciation for people under extreme circumstances. They had a feeling of acceptance from him. He felt neither judgement or fear. He could get along with chimney sweeps or royalty.” With those big, spherical eyes that took in everything and a face that would assume a persona to go with every social setting, Brassaï was just as much in his element whether he was socialising in the smart neighbourhoods, during elegant gatherings, or in the “slaughterhouse” brothels – or really wherever in the city where the old ways were challenged by the nightcrawlers and their push towards unknown pleasures.

It is not without reason that Brassaï called himself a “plunderer of beauty of all kinds”. The graffiti images aside, it is solely the “chimney sweep” population of the city, along with the strange and dreamy night views like his wet and mysterious Paving Stones at Night (ca 1931–32), Pont Neuf in the Snow (ca 1934–35) with the gleaming trees in the foreground, or the ghostly Statue of Marshal Ney in the Fog (1932) with that Hotel sign suspended somewhere in the back of the gloominess – that compose all the other gorgeous prints in The Secret Signs of Paris.

“His vision penetrated to the simplest yet deepest truths about people and things,” writes Jean-Claude Gautrand in Brassaï Paris. “[All] of his media was driven by the same basic goal: he wanted to create a sort of encyclopaedia of human life. And he never played tricks with the truth.”

Brassaï’s pictures of people joined in a smooch bring human life to light. His sprightly Kiss on a Swing at a Street Fair (ca 1935–37) shows an infatuated couple and their sweet communion of a kiss at that fraction of a second when the cart hits zero gravity and love is perfect. Then we have the boulevard kisses, the bistro kisses, the bar kisses, the ball kisses – and as Brassaï described it in The Secret Paris of the 30s: “The dancehalls were full of poetry and dreams, but they were also full of pitfalls: true love came close to prostitution. In these dancehalls, young pimps seduced girls and recruited the labour force for the streets and the whorehouses.”

The Secret Signs of Paris shows the Eiffel Tower as a rocket from an illuminated past when it carried André Citroën’s logo on three of its sides, formed by a quarter of a million bulbs; the clochards and the bargemen down by the Seine; the meat porters and the streetwalkers around the old and forever lost Les Halles; the Morris columns and the pissotières (urinals) (“Neither the smell nor the dirt of these places repulsed the devotees of Greek love. On the contrary. The more malodorous the chapels, the more popular they became”) and, certainly, his iconic picture of the Steps of Montmartre (ca 1937) on top of rue Foyatier and one can only imagine Brassaï standing there, out of breath, after having started the climb from the never-ending spiral staircase at the nearby Abbesses metro station.

Two further examples of Brassaï’s early mastery of the photographic medium is his night shot of Edmond Lévêque’s sculpture Diana the Huntress in the Tuileries Garden (1931), in what he makes from the little light around and that strange maze of bare branches behind the Roman goddess. The other one is “La Cage aux fauves”, Scene at the Folies-Bergère (ca 1932) with a dozen of glamorous (though not particularly wild) showgirls who are lying half-naked on the floor of a cage like pieces of hors d’oeuvres from a surrealistic nocturnal discharge.

Brassaï encountered La Môme Bijou in a bar in Montmartre in the middle of the night at the beginning of 1932. He took three pictures (which was his fixed limit) of her and never saw her again. This “ageless” woman in her tattered turn-of-the-century garments who looks at us at the Moderna does have the appearance of an Xmas arrangement gone wrong. “Mlle Diamonds” was indeed a heap of cheap glitter and too much of everything else, but not of herself which makes this portrait another Brassaï classic.

The picture of Fat Claude from the same year is showing Violette Morris as a crossdresser at the lesbian nightclub Le Monocle, and she is possessively touching a very feminine woman’s elbow at a table. After Morris had become a discus and shotput world champion in the 1920s, she had her breasts removed and then transformed herself into La grosse Claude – a nasty figure who, after appearing as a guest of honour at the 1936 Olympics in Berlin, became a Gestapo collaborator who fancied beating up female prisoners of war. Morris was assassinated by the Resistance in 1944.

There are of course a couple of prints of the Queen of Montparnasse too, and you can sense the photographer’s love for her in these pictures and how he spelled it out: “Kiki [de Montparnasse] raised immodesty to an art. Her wit was equally uncorseted. Totally spontaneous, frank without the slightest trace of hypocrisy, she called things by their names. She never avoided vulgar words, but when she spoke them in her fresh, innocent voice, they lost all their vulgarity and even took on a kind of nobility.”

When Kiki collapsed on the street in the spring of 1953, after a life of alcohol and cocaine dependency, she wasn’t even as old as the century. The painter Tsuguharu Foujita was the only one who attended the funeral. Foujita mourned his lifelong friend and he mourned that “the glorious days of Montparnasse were buried forever”.

Nina Bouraoui is treating words as bodies without organs in the Stockholm catalogue and contends that “Brassaï delivers us characters untarnished by the passing of time, characters who could be part of today’s underground scene.” This habit of blotting things past with contemporary rubbish and invalid ideology is the ticket for the fools and the frauds who cannot or will not care for anything deep and necessary.

“Look again at that dot,” urged Carl Sagan in his book Pale Blue Dot (1994), startled by that incredible picture acquired by Voyager 1 on February 14, 1990: “On it everyone you love, everyone you know, everyone you ever heard of, every human being who ever was, lived out their lives. The aggregate of our joy and suffering, thousands of confident religions, ideologies, and economic doctrines, every hunter and forager, every hero and coward, every creator and destroyer of civilisation, every king and peasant, every young couple in love, every mother and father, hopeful child, inventor and explorer, every teacher of morals, every corrupt politician, every superstar, every supreme leader, every saint and sinner in the history of our species lived there on a mote of dust suspended in a sunbeam.”

It is abundantly clear how Brassaï’s from-dusk-to-dawn photography of the Parisian underworld managed to pull out this whole existential magnificence from a tellurian point of view, sixty years earlier. His images of unwonted human presence of yesteryear, suspended in time, are in equal shares about the unconventional fauna of humanity and about finding a speck of fellowship among others. What’s “us”. And as the Moderna Museet show makes you wonder: almost a century later there are enough and to spare of the pretenders, crooks and destroyers, while the prettiest stars stay engraved in your memory.

Tintin Törncrantz

Brassaï: The Secret Signs of Parisat the Moderna Museet in Stockholm through October 4, 2026.

Published by Kehrer Verlag, “Unspoken”by Jo Ann Chaususes staged self-portraits to explore womanhood and self-empowerment.

Over the course of more than a decade, Unspoken evolved from the artist’s private exchange with her camera into a profound visual investigation of identity. In this series, Jo Ann Chaus embodies a range of female stereotypes and archetypes figures shaped by inherited expectations and internalized roles. Though a modern, independent woman, the artist came to recognize how deeply she remained bound to her mother’s generation, guided by the ideals of the devoted wife and self-sacrificing mother. Her photo series, in which vintage garments and objects link private narrative to collective cultural memory, exposes the tension between what was expected of her and what she became and is.

From the prologue by Debra Klomp Ching:

Over the course of the series, autobiography diminishes to a certain extent, and the subject in the frame shifts from a representation of a seemingly unobtainable self to an homage to all women the universality of the burdens of wife and mother, the self-sacrifice of personal desire for the better of others, and a suggestion of the possibility of unfulfilled potential being acknowledged. While these photographs are undeniably about her, and for her she allows the viewer the possibility of supplanting Chaus with ourselves. We (women) merge with and are her.

Jo Ann Chaus is a New York–based artist. In her photographic work, she draws on the visual traditions of early color photography, drawing particular inspiration from William Eggleston and Saul Leiter. Through her striking use of color and light, she directs attention to the ambiguous and the metaphorical in her self-portraits, landscapes, and still lifes. Chaus studied at the International Center of Photography and Maine Media College. Before her artistic career, she worked in the fashion industry. Her work has been exhibited nationally and internationally and has received numerous awards.

Debra Klomp Ching is co-owner of the Klompching Gallery in New York. She also works as an independent consultant, writer, curator, and lecturer. She has served on the jury of numerous renowned photography awards, including the Arnold Newman Portrait Award (2018), and is co-founder of the Rhonda Wilson Award. She also teaches as an adjunct lecturer at the School of Visual Arts in New York.

Holidays – a time to put your everyday worries aside for a while and see things from a different angle, such as visiting a non-photographic exhibition… and there to rediscover new perspectives from which to approach the medium of photography critically…

Leon Spilliaert (1881–1946) was a Belgian artist associated with Symbolism. He was born in Ostend, grew up there and also worked there during what was arguably the most innovative and surprising period of his career. Later in life, he moved to Brussels.

He produced a significant part of his body of work in the privacy of his (parental) home, or at night whilst walking along the harbour, the beach or the seafront. All his works are, in essence, still lifes, even when human figures appear.

At the PATRICK DEROM GALLERY, an exhibition of some 40 works by Leon Spilliaert is currently on display for a few more days, many of which are being shown to the general public for the first time in a long while.

The exhibition opens with a realistic drawing by the 18-year-old Spilliaert, who is peering into the laboratory in the attic room of his father, a perfumer. On the door, a Japanese-style advertising poster captures the spirit of the times for ‘Eau Kadsura’, a creation by Spilliaert senior. On the other side is a drawing that appears to be a parody of ‘Self-Portrait with the Flower Hat’ (1883–88) by fellow Ostend artist James Ensor (1860–1949). It is a homely, unpretentious image, yet one that tells a story of the spirit of the times, whilst also offering a hint at human relationships, for through the door we catch a glimpse of a devil’s mask with a set of scales. Reality or symbolism?

The exhibition at Derom Gallery features some 40 works, mainly still lifes of simple objects. Teacups, teapots, a clock, bottles, vials and flasks. It inevitably brings to mind that other artist, Morandi (1890–1964), and Joël Meyerowitz’s (1938) publication Morandi’s Objects, but with one major difference. Morandi’s objects stand alone, in an abstract space, and relate solely to themselves. In Spilliaert’s work, they are situated within a space; they reflect the other objects in their surroundings and the light, yet they also allude to the owners of the objects. In this sense, the objects become portraits, rather than exercises in abstraction.

Spilliaert created his images in the privacy of his own home, and yet he grants us a glimpse out in The Glass Roof (1909). One cannot help but think of the works produced in the 1920s and 1930s by European and American modernist photographers such as Charles Sheeler (1883–1965), in which the straight lines of the urban and industrial environment dominate the image.

In a separate room, a further seven works by Spilliaert are on display, including “Ghost Ship”. It dates from a period in which Spilliaert was searching for a new visual language, and produced a number of works in (almost) monochrome blue, such as 1924’s “Jeunes filles à la plage”. One cannot help but think he was influenced by cyanotype – or how there is a constant interplay between the various forms of expression… Nothing stands still; everything interacts.

Many photographers appreciate Spilliaert’s work; I would also like to mention the marvellous exhibition by Dirk Braeckman juxtaposed with Leon Spilliaert (Night Wanderers) at the Kunstmuseum in The Hague in 2024–25, the splendid catalogue of which is now only available second-hand.

Don’t worry, though, as the catalogue Leon Spilliaert Interiors and Still Lifes is more than worth the reading effort. It was published in three editions – Dutch, French and English – by Hannibal Books, edited by Anne Adriaens-Pannier and Edouard Derom, with fine contributions from the aforementioned authors as well as, for example, Stefan Huyghebaert, who reconstructed the artist’s living space.

Conclusion: this is an exhibition we would go so far as to describe as ‘worth going to’.In particular, for all photographers who feel the need to describe themselves as ‘Art Photographers’ or ‘High Art Photographers’. Beauty and art lie not in the intention but in the image. Whether in a documentary image (think HCB), still lifes or photographers’ personal creations… Next time I’ll talk exclusively about photography, I promise!

John Devos

Johndevos.photo at gmail.com

Jayne H Baum – JHB Gallery presents a selection of photographs by Yuki Onodera.

“Yuki Onodera is a Japanese photographer who has lived in Paris since 1993. Her work explores the concepts of floating and weightlessness by means of technical and artistic experimentation.

In the series ‘Portraits of Second-Hand Clothes’, she photographed clothes she acquired during an exhibition by the artist Christian Boltanski, at which visitors could buy bags of second-hand clothing. She set these fabrics against a background of sky, making them resemble cloudy, disembodied portraits. For her project ‘P.N.I’ (standing for ‘portraits non identifiés’, or unidentified portraits), she collaged together eyes, noses and mouths from the faces of unknown people she found in magazines. Finding the structure in these soft-focus compositions demands a certain amount of effort on the part of the viewer.

Other projects have involved creating extremely large-format silkscreen prints, sometimes more than two metres in height; the manipulation of images via the use of collage and double exposures; the transformation of video clips into static images; and the staging of fictional scenes. Whatever she does, Onodera continues to push the boundaries of photography practice.”

From: Clara Bouveresse, Women Photographers: Contemporaries, 1970-today, Thames & Hudson, 2020.

Yuki Onodera was born in Tokyo, Japan in 1962 and lives and works in Paris, France.

Jayne H Baum – JHB Gallery

26 Grove Street Suite #4C

New York, NY 10014

Image 59: Book: 'Bell Pond' documents the summer of 1983 at a public swimming pond in Worcester, Massachusetts, where Stephen DiRado spent months photographing the community that gathered there. Arriving one afternoon on a whim, in the midst of an early heat wave, he introduced himself to anyone who would give him the time of day, and he returned day after day. By the end of the summer, DiRado had become a familiar figure, his daily arrival an event in itself. @stephenphotodirado @tbwbooks Photo: Cheryl, Jamie and Michael © Stephen DiRad - Bell Pond - Courtesy TBW Books — — — — — Livre : 'Bell Pond' documente l’été 1983 dans un étang de baignade public à Worcester, dans le Massachusetts, où DiRado a passé des mois à photographier la communauté qui s’y retrouvait. Arrivé un après-midi sur un coup de tête, en pleine canicule précoce, il s’est présenté à quiconque voulait bien lui prêter attention, et il est revenu, jour après jour. À la fin de l’été, DiRado était devenu une figure familière, son arrivée quotidienne un événement en soi. #tbwbooks #stephendirado #photobook

Image 61: The Questionnaire : There are photographers who show us the world. Klavdij Sluban belongs to that much rarer breed who question it. For him, photography does not document; it clarifies. It seeks neither proof nor spectacle, nor even the decisive moment. It moves against the tide of time, at a deliberately unhurried pace, until reality ceases to be an obvious fact and becomes a question. @klavdijsluban A column by @carole.schmitz Photo: Divagation - sur les pas de Basho, Ferry vers Hokkaidon, Japon, 2016 © Klavdij Sluban — — — — — Le Questionnaire : Il existe des photographes qui montrent le monde. Klavdij Sluban appartient à cette famille beaucoup plus rare de ceux qui le mettent en doute. Chez lui, la photographie ne documente pas, elle décante. Elle ne cherche ni la preuve, ni le spectaculaire, ni même l’instant décisif. Elle avance à contretemps, dans une lenteur revendiquée, jusqu’à ce que le réel cesse d’être une évidence pour devenir une question. #klavdijsluban #caroleschmitz #lequestionnaire

Image 63: Our Week Favorite: This is a journey invented by mind, with the images, people, and memories that inhabit it. It is a notebook of deepest fantasies, pâle because they have been faded by time and memory. Origini chases black and old looking style, using materials and colours that aspire to the universal— without place and without time: Gabrielle’s eye has no time. Her photographs could have been taken sixty years ago or yesterday — that’s her magic. @gabrielleduplantier @originiedizioni Photo: © Gabrielle Duplantier — — — — — Notre sélection de la semaine : C’est un voyage imaginé par l’esprit, peuplé d’images, de personnages et de souvenirs. C’est un carnet de notes où s’inscrivent les fantasmes les plus profonds, pâles car estompés par le temps et la mémoire. 'Origini' privilégie un style sombre et vintage, en utilisant des matériaux et des couleurs qui aspirent à l’universel — hors lieu et hors temps : le regard de Gabrielle est intemporel. Ses photographies auraient pu être prises il y a soixante ans ou hier — c’est là toute sa magie. #originiedizioni #gabrielleduplantier

Image 65: Portfolio : “This book was created during a period of returning home—both physically and emotionally. After years spent living abroad, I came back to the place I grew up, carrying a lifetime of experiences, loss, and unanswered questions. What began as an attempt to document my surroundings slowly became something more personal. The photographs turned inward. The writing followed. The house, the landscape, the quiet moments—they became a way of understanding memory, grief, and healing.” @arthurmeehanphotography Photo: © Arthur Meehan — — — — — Portfolio : « Après avoir passé plusieurs années à l’étranger, je suis revenue dans la ville où j’ai grandi, chargée d’une vie d’expériences, de pertes et de questions sans réponse. Ce qui avait commencé comme une tentative de documenter mon environnement s’est peu à peu transformé en quelque chose de plus personnel. Les photographies se sont tournées vers l’intériorité. Les textes ont suivi. La maison, le paysage, les moments de calme… tout cela est devenu un moyen de comprendre la mémoire, le deuil et la guérison ». Comme Arthur Meehan, envoyez-nous vos portfolios. #portfolio #arthurmeehan

Image 67: Portfolio: ‘Pacific Insomnia’ is an ongoing photographic series shot in French Polynesia. Every year, travelling funfairs stop off in Tahiti for a few weeks before moving on. For many of the island’s inhabitants, they offer a rare form of entertainment and form an integral part of a seasonal ritual. Like Hélène Havard, send us your portfolios. @helenehavard_travel Photo: © Hélène Havard Portfolio : « Pacific Insomnia » est une série photographique en cours réalisée en Polynésie française. Chaque année, des fêtes foraines itinérantes font escale à Tahiti pendant quelques semaines avant de repartir. Pour de nombreux habitants de l’île, elles constituent un divertissement rare et font partie intégrante d’un rituel saisonnier. Comme Hélène Havard, envoyez-nous vos portfolios. #portfolio #helenehavard

Image 69: Exhibition: Jerry Schatzberg belongs to a rare group of photographers who understood that performance does not begin on stage or end when the curtain falls. In his photographs, the worlds of music, fashion, dance, and celebrity are never reduced to publicity or pose. They appear instead through gesture, rhythm, atmosphere, and presence. On view at Holden Luntz Gallery. @schatzbergarchive @onlyediesedgwick @holdenluntzgallery Photo: Jerry Schatzberg, Edie Sedgwick, Slash, New York 1966, Silver Gelatin Photograph © Jerry Schatzberg - Courtesy Holden Luntz Gallery — — — — — Exposition : Jerry Schatzberg appartient à ce groupe restreint de photographes qui ont compris que la performance ne commence pas sur scène et ne s’achève pas à la tombée du rideau. Dans ses photographies, les mondes de la musique, de la mode, de la danse et de la célébrité ne se réduisent jamais à la publicité ou à la pose. Ils se révèlent au contraire à travers le geste, le rythme, l’atmosphère et la présence. #jerryschatzberg #ediesedgwick #holdenluntz

Image 71: Portfolio: On view for eleven days on the walls of the Ramallah Contemporary Arts Festival 2026, Mélissa Waucquier’s Fair Mur is a public photographic installation comprising portraits, rehearsal scenes and candid moments. @melissa_waucquier Photo: Melissa Waucquier, from the series 'Faire Mur', 2026, Ramal lah Contemporary Arts Festival 2026 © Melissa Waucquier — — — — — Portfolio: Deployée pendant onze jours sur les murs du Ramallah Contemporary Arts Festival 2026, Fair Mur de Mélissa Waucquier est une installation photographique ouverte au public, composée de portraits, de scènes de répétition et d’instantanés. #ramallah #melissawaucquier

Image 79: Book: 'Night Journey' was meticulously staged by Susan Kae Grant in her studio. Here, she acts as a shadow theater director orchestrating scenes that are devoid of color and evocative of fairy tales, nightmares, and—probably—Plato’s allegory of the cave. A book published by MW Editions. @susankaegrant @mweditions Photo: Amelia’s Phantom, 2012 © Susan kae Grant - Night Journey - Courtesy MW Editions — — — — — Livre : « Night Journey » a été mis en scène avec minutie par Susan Kae Grant dans son atelier. Elle y endosse le rôle de metteuse en scène de théâtre d’ombres, orchestrant des scènes dépourvues de couleur qui évoquent les contes de fées, les cauchemars et — sans doute — l’allégorie de la caverne de Platon. Un ouvrage publié par MW Editions.

Image 81: Book: 'SACA 1504' by Manuel Naranjo Martell is a photobook on an ancestral ritual that forms part of America’s equestrian roots. The photobook highlights the yegüerizos as essential bearers of a form of knowledge transmitted orally and through the body—deeply bound to both the horse and the landscape of Doñana. Published by Editorial RM. @manuelnaranjomartell @editorial_rm Photo: © Manuel Naranjo Martell — — — — — Livre : « SACA 1504 », de Manuel Naranjo Martell est un livre de photographies consacré à un rituel ancestral qui s'inscrit dans les racines équestres de l'Amérique. Cet ouvrage met en lumière les yegüerizos, gardiens incontournables d'un savoir transmis oralement et par le corps, profondément lié à la fois au cheval et au paysage de Doñana. Publié par Editorial RM. #photobook #manuelnaranjomartell

Image 83: Podcast: Regularly, photographer Maud Bernos interviews a woman photographer to discuss her career in photography, her creative processes, her influences, feminism and her commitment as a woman photographer. In her last episode, she discuss the work of Flore Prébay in French. @maud_bernos @flobayphoto Photo: Multivers, de la série Deuil blanc © Flore Prébay — — — — — Podcast: La photographe Maud Bernos interviewe régulièrement une femme photographe pour évoquer son parcours dans la photographie, ses processus créatifs, ses influences, le féminisme et son engagement en tant que femme photographe. Dans son dernier épisode, elle aborde le travail de Flore Prébay en français. #maudbernos #floreprebay

Image 85: Portfolio: The work is set in the historic fishing district of Hastings, on the south coast of England. This setting plays a central role. The net shops, fishermen’s huts and the large car park reserved for visitors, set against the constant force of the English Channel, create a striking contrast that shapes the atmosphere of the images. Like Andreas Bleckmann, send us your portfolios. @andreasbleckmannphotos Photo: © Andreas Bleckmann — — — — — Portfolio : Le travail se déroule dans le quartier historique des pêcheurs de Hastings, sur la côte sud de l’Angleterre. Ce cadre joue un rôle central. Les magasins de filets, les cabanes de pêcheurs et le grand parking réservé aux visiteurs, face à la force constante de la Manche, créent un contraste saisissant qui façonne l’atmosphère des images. Comme Andreas Bleckmann, envoyez-nous vos portfolios.

Image 87: The Book Column: Here, they say the earth is ‘in love’ when it sticks to your boots. It observes the actions through which a landscape is shaped and the way in which bodies transform their environment just as much as they are transformed by it. Image 59: Book: 'Bell Pond' documents the summer of 1983 at a public swimming pond in Worcester, Massachusetts, where Stephen DiRado spent months photographing the community that gathered there. Arriving one afternoon on a whim, in the midst of an early heat wave, he introduced himself to anyone who would give him the time of day, and he returned day after day. By the end of the summer, DiRado had become a familiar figure, his daily arrival an event in itself. @stephenphotodirado @tbwbooks Photo: Cheryl, Jamie and Michael © Stephen DiRad - Bell Pond - Courtesy TBW Books — — — — — Livre : 'Bell Pond' documente l’été 1983 dans un étang de baignade public à Worcester, dans le Massachusetts, où DiRado a passé des mois à photographier la communauté qui s’y retrouvait. Arrivé un après-midi sur un coup de tête, en pleine canicule précoce, il s’est présenté à quiconque voulait bien lui prêter attention, et il est revenu, jour après jour. À la fin de l’été, DiRado était devenu une figure familière, son arrivée quotidienne un événement en soi. #tbwbooks #stephendirado #photobook

Image 61: The Questionnaire : There are photographers who show us the world. Klavdij Sluban belongs to that much rarer breed who question it. For him, photography does not document; it clarifies. It seeks neither proof nor spectacle, nor even the decisive moment. It moves against the tide of time, at a deliberately unhurried pace, until reality ceases to be an obvious fact and becomes a question. @klavdijsluban A column by @carole.schmitz Photo: Divagation - sur les pas de Basho, Ferry vers Hokkaidon, Japon, 2016 © Klavdij Sluban — — — — — Le Questionnaire : Il existe des photographes qui montrent le monde. Klavdij Sluban appartient à cette famille beaucoup plus rare de ceux qui le mettent en doute. Chez lui, la photographie ne documente pas, elle décante. Elle ne cherche ni la preuve, ni le spectaculaire, ni même l’instant décisif. Elle avance à contretemps, dans une lenteur revendiquée, jusqu’à ce que le réel cesse d’être une évidence pour devenir une question. #klavdijsluban #caroleschmitz #lequestionnaire

Image 63: Our Week Favorite: This is a journey invented by mind, with the images, people, and memories that inhabit it. It is a notebook of deepest fantasies, pâle because they have been faded by time and memory. Origini chases black and old looking style, using materials and colours that aspire to the universal— without place and without time: Gabrielle’s eye has no time. Her photographs could have been taken sixty years ago or yesterday — that’s her magic. @gabrielleduplantier @originiedizioni Photo: © Gabrielle Duplantier — — — — — Notre sélection de la semaine : C’est un voyage imaginé par l’esprit, peuplé d’images, de personnages et de souvenirs. C’est un carnet de notes où s’inscrivent les fantasmes les plus profonds, pâles car estompés par le temps et la mémoire. 'Origini' privilégie un style sombre et vintage, en utilisant des matériaux et des couleurs qui aspirent à l’universel — hors lieu et hors temps : le regard de Gabrielle est intemporel. Ses photographies auraient pu être prises il y a soixante ans ou hier — c’est là toute sa magie. #originiedizioni #gabrielleduplantier

Image 65: Portfolio : “This book was created during a period of returning home—both physically and emotionally. After years spent living abroad, I came back to the place I grew up, carrying a lifetime of experiences, loss, and unanswered questions. What began as an attempt to document my surroundings slowly became something more personal. The photographs turned inward. The writing followed. The house, the landscape, the quiet moments—they became a way of understanding memory, grief, and healing.” @arthurmeehanphotography Photo: © Arthur Meehan — — — — — Portfolio : « Après avoir passé plusieurs années à l’étranger, je suis revenue dans la ville où j’ai grandi, chargée d’une vie d’expériences, de pertes et de questions sans réponse. Ce qui avait commencé comme une tentative de documenter mon environnement s’est peu à peu transformé en quelque chose de plus personnel. Les photographies se sont tournées vers l’intériorité. Les textes ont suivi. La maison, le paysage, les moments de calme… tout cela est devenu un moyen de comprendre la mémoire, le deuil et la guérison ». Comme Arthur Meehan, envoyez-nous vos portfolios. #portfolio #arthurmeehan

Image 67: Portfolio: ‘Pacific Insomnia’ is an ongoing photographic series shot in French Polynesia. Every year, travelling funfairs stop off in Tahiti for a few weeks before moving on. For many of the island’s inhabitants, they offer a rare form of entertainment and form an integral part of a seasonal ritual. Like Hélène Havard, send us your portfolios. @helenehavard_travel Photo: © Hélène Havard Portfolio : « Pacific Insomnia » est une série photographique en cours réalisée en Polynésie française. Chaque année, des fêtes foraines itinérantes font escale à Tahiti pendant quelques semaines avant de repartir. Pour de nombreux habitants de l’île, elles constituent un divertissement rare et font partie intégrante d’un rituel saisonnier. Comme Hélène Havard, envoyez-nous vos portfolios. #portfolio #helenehavard

Image 69: Exhibition: Jerry Schatzberg belongs to a rare group of photographers who understood that performance does not begin on stage or end when the curtain falls. In his photographs, the worlds of music, fashion, dance, and celebrity are never reduced to publicity or pose. They appear instead through gesture, rhythm, atmosphere, and presence. On view at Holden Luntz Gallery. @schatzbergarchive @onlyediesedgwick @holdenluntzgallery Photo: Jerry Schatzberg, Edie Sedgwick, Slash, New York 1966, Silver Gelatin Photograph © Jerry Schatzberg - Courtesy Holden Luntz Gallery — — — — — Exposition : Jerry Schatzberg appartient à ce groupe restreint de photographes qui ont compris que la performance ne commence pas sur scène et ne s’achève pas à la tombée du rideau. Dans ses photographies, les mondes de la musique, de la mode, de la danse et de la célébrité ne se réduisent jamais à la publicité ou à la pose. Ils se révèlent au contraire à travers le geste, le rythme, l’atmosphère et la présence. #jerryschatzberg #ediesedgwick #holdenluntz

Image 79: Book: 'Night Journey' was meticulously staged by Susan Kae Grant in her studio. Here, she acts as a shadow theater director orchestrating scenes that are devoid of color and evocative of fairy tales, nightmares, and—probably—Plato’s allegory of the cave. A book published by MW Editions. @susankaegrant @mweditions Photo: Amelia’s Phantom, 2012 © Susan kae Grant - Night Journey - Courtesy MW Editions — — — — — Livre : « Night Journey » a été mis en scène avec minutie par Susan Kae Grant dans son atelier. Elle y endosse le rôle de metteuse en scène de théâtre d’ombres, orchestrant des scènes dépourvues de couleur qui évoquent les contes de fées, les cauchemars et — sans doute — l’allégorie de la caverne de Platon. Un ouvrage publié par MW Editions.

Image 81: Book: 'SACA 1504' by Manuel Naranjo Martell is a photobook on an ancestral ritual that forms part of America’s equestrian roots. The photobook highlights the yegüerizos as essential bearers of a form of knowledge transmitted orally and through the body—deeply bound to both the horse and the landscape of Doñana. Published by Editorial RM. @manuelnaranjomartell @editorial_rm Photo: © Manuel Naranjo Martell — — — — — Livre : « SACA 1504 », de Manuel Naranjo Martell est un livre de photographies consacré à un rituel ancestral qui s'inscrit dans les racines équestres de l'Amérique. Cet ouvrage met en lumière les yegüerizos, gardiens incontournables d'un savoir transmis oralement et par le corps, profondément lié à la fois au cheval et au paysage de Doñana. Publié par Editorial RM. #photobook #manuelnaranjomartell

Image 83: Podcast: Regularly, photographer Maud Bernos interviews a woman photographer to discuss her career in photography, her creative processes, her influences, feminism and her commitment as a woman photographer. In her last episode, she discuss the work of Flore Prébay in French. @maud_bernos @flobayphoto Photo: Multivers, de la série Deuil blanc © Flore Prébay — — — — — Podcast: La photographe Maud Bernos interviewe régulièrement une femme photographe pour évoquer son parcours dans la photographie, ses processus créatifs, ses influences, le féminisme et son engagement en tant que femme photographe. Dans son dernier épisode, elle aborde le travail de Flore Prébay en français. #maudbernos #floreprebay

Image 85: Portfolio: The work is set in the historic fishing district of Hastings, on the south coast of England. This setting plays a central role. The net shops, fishermen’s huts and the large car park reserved for visitors, set against the constant force of the English Channel, create a striking contrast that shapes the atmosphere of the images. Like Andreas Bleckmann, send us your portfolios. @andreasbleckmannphotos Photo: © Andreas Bleckmann — — — — — Portfolio : Le travail se déroule dans le quartier historique des pêcheurs de Hastings, sur la côte sud de l’Angleterre. Ce cadre joue un rôle central. Les magasins de filets, les cabanes de pêcheurs et le grand parking réservé aux visiteurs, face à la force constante de la Manche, créent un contraste saisissant qui façonne l’atmosphère des images. Comme Andreas Bleckmann, envoyez-nous vos portfolios.

Archives – August 12, 2022

James Hyman Gallery presented recently the very first London exhibition of one of the greatest figures in the history of photography, the Countess of Castiglione.

This major solo exhibition includes over fifty rare portraits of the Countess from the 1850s to the 1890s. Directed and staged by the Countess, herself, and created in collaboration with the studio photographer Pierre-Louis Pierson, these “self-portraits” are some of the most extraordinary pictures in the history of photography, precursors to fashion photography and performative self-portraiture.

Today, we live in a world of selfies and social media: an Instagram world of constructed identities, performance, and disguise. But before all this, before super-models and influencers – 150 years ago – one of the most radical figures of the nineteenth century was pioneering new forms of fashion and conceptual photography: autofiction. In hundreds of portraits produced over a period of decades the Countess staged scenarios and performed different roles, to present different characters and personalities and to reflect multiple, fluid, unfixed identities.

Despite decades of activity, photographs by the Countess are incredibly rare as very few prints were made and she chose not to distribute. In fact, major exhibitions of her work only took place at the end of the 20th century at the Musée d’Orsay, Paris in 1999 and then at the Metropolitan Museum, New York in 2000. Most of her work is now in the Collection of the Metropolitan Museum.

The exhibition presents some of the most famous images of the Countess as well as an exquisite, recently- discovered painted photograph of her which will be exhibited for the very first time.

The exhibition includes vintage prints as well as prints specially made in 1900 for her great admirer, the symbolist poet Robert Montesquiou, who spent thirteen years of his life writing her biography, which was published as La Divine Comtesse in 1913.

James Hyman writes:

“I’m really excited to stage this special exhibition by arguably the most contemporary of all nineteenth-century photographers. I’m passionate about early photographers such as William Henry Fox Talbot, Roger Fenton, Julia Margaret Cameron, Charles Negre and Gustave le Gray, but, for me, no one is more influential or relevant to today’s photographers than the Countess of Castiglione.

The Countess is arguably the most radical and contemporary photographer of the nineteenth century. Today, her relevance is everywhere. She stands at the start of a line of conceptual, performative, inventive self-portraitists such as Claude Cahun, Francesca Woodman, Hannah Wilkie, Jo Spence, Sophie Calle, Gillian Wearing, Cindy Sherman and Tracey Emin, and is an inspiration for numerous younger artists, among them Zanele Muholi and Heather Agyepong.

The work is incredibly rare making this an important opportunity for collectors to acquire such important works.”

The portraits come from three main periods: 1856–57, 1861–67, and 1893–95 and the exhibition takes us on a journey from the Countess in her prime – costumed and fetishised as the most beautiful woman of her age, through images in which she attempted to reclaim former triumphs, to emotionally charged late images which suggest not just the fading of her beauty but also psychological trauma. After the glamourous masquerades of her early photographs, these harrowing later pictures provide a devastating portrayal of loss and ageing.

All works are for sale subject to availability. Prices range from £4,000 – £55,000

The Countess of Castiglione. The Creation of a Legend9 June – 26 August 2022

James Hyman Gallery50 Maddox Street

London, W1S 1AY

www.jameshymangallery.com

Archives – August 12, 2020

Daniel Blau presents Backstage and Kammerspiele– an exhibition comprising Margaret Bourke-White’sbackstage photographs of burlesque dancers shown alongside the 1920s theatrical pictures of Li Osborne (1883-1968).

Bourke-White’s sensual photographs of Broadway burlesque performers give us a glimpse of New York’s entertainment world in the mid 1930s. The subjects of these striking photos are New York’s chorus girls and performers as they prepare their makeup and costumes and wait to go onstage. In one extraordinary picture we see three ballerinas of the Ballet Russe reclining in extravagant tutus as a ﬁreman looks on. In other works we are privy to moments in the wings and beneath stage lights as the women perform for unseen audiences.The prints feature original captions and press stamps on the verso.

Margaret Bourke-White (1904 – 1971) is known for her pioneering photojournalism. She was born in New York City in 1904 and grew up in New Jersey. After studying science and art she became an industrial photographer, takeing signiﬁcant pictures of factories and architecture before joining prestigious magazines such as Fortune and LIFE as a photographer. She travelled and photographed extensively, covering major international events from World War II to the partition of India and Pakistan.

Performance and the human form are also the focus of the 1920s Kammerspiele pictures by German photographer and sculptor Li Osborne (née Luisa Friedericke Susanna Wolf). The gallery is showing Osborne’s vintage pictures of imaginative Kammerspiele set designs – hand drawn and evocative visualisations – as well as performance stills from productions at the Kammerspiele theatre that capture the charisma and energy of individual performers and moments of action onstage.

Li Osborne moved to Munich in 1925 where she photographed cultural ﬁgures such as Bertolt Brecht. She emigrated to Switzerland in 1934 due to the rise of Nazism and later began a new career as a self-taught sculptor and moved to England where she worked under the name Louise Hutchinson-Wolf. The Kammerspiele was founded in 1906 in Schwabing as a private theatre troupe and later became Munich’s municipal theatre company. Falckenberg, the producer-director during Osborne’s time, was regarded as an authority on Expressionism in Germany during the Weimar Republic and produced many celebrated productions at the company including Brecht’s ﬁrst staged play, Drums in the Night, in 1922.

The exhibition shows two women artists’ perspectives on two very different performance contexts in the US and Germany in the years between the World Wars.

Margaret Bourke-White – Backstage – Burlesque 1936Li Osborne – Photographs Of “Münchener Kammerspiele” From the 1920sJuly 30 – September 8, 2020

Indian photographer Aman Alam presents a solo exhibition at Les Rencontres d’Arles, following his selection as the recipient of the 2025 Serendipity Arles Grant.

Alam’s exhibition, Ozymandias(2020–ongoing), is an intimate and multidisciplinary body of work that examines memory, identity, and cognitive decline through the artist’s experience of caring for his grandmother after she was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease. Drawing on photography, sculpture, machine intelligence, and family archives, the project explores what it means to remember, to forget, and to care for someone whose sense of self is gradually eroding. Named after Percy Bysshe Shelley’s 1818 poem on the impermanence of human achievement, Ozymandias reflects on the fragility of memory and the emotional realities of caregiving.

Aman would be delighted to discuss the personal experience that informed the project, and his wider practice, which often explores how intimate human stories can illuminate broader social and emotional realities.

The Serendipity Arles Grant was launched in 2020 by Serendipity Arts, an international not-for-profit cultural organisation based in India. Best known for the Serendipity Arts Festival in Goa, South Asia’s largest multidisciplinary arts festival, the organisation supports artists year-round through grants, residencies, commissions, and international partnerships (most recently they were a partner of the India Pavilion at the Venice Biennale). The grant is the largest of its kind for lens-based practitioners from South Asia, creating opportunities for artists from the region to present new work on an international stage.

This Wednesday, August 12, 2026, will no doubt have left its mark on the minds of our fellow citizens as a chapter of our contemporary history: a solar eclipse was there for all to see.

They came in great numbers, with their families — nearly two hundred people — to observe it at the spot known as “la découverte,” the Place du Forum in Daix, a small Burgundian commune in the Côte-d’Or, part of the Dijon metropolitan area.

The Astro Daix association, founded just three years ago by André Louis Roy, a Daix resident passionate about astronomy, brings together about a dozen lovers of the sky and space. It invited anyone interested — equipped with special ISO 12312-2 certified glasses to protect against the highly harmful rays that burn the retina without one noticing — to come and experience a magical, once-in-a-lifetime moment, in which the moon’s shadow covers part of the sun, here in Burgundy 92% of the solar disk.

The phenomenon is so rare and striking that it can’t be missed! Once or twice in a lifetime.

The sun is 400 times larger than the moon, and likewise 400 times farther away.

Philippe Saison, an association member and Astro Daix facilitator, remotely operated his automated Seestar S50 telescope fitted with a special filter. The telescope allowed him to photograph and record, sequentially and without risk, the progress of the solar eclipse, which lasted about two hours — though in Burgundy, as elsewhere in France, it was not possible to see “the black sun.”

Another telescope, this one a manually operated Skywatcher Dobsonian 135-900mm, was also set up on-site, and both instruments were fitted with special filters to observe the solar eclipse.

The next eclipse will be a lunar one, on August 28, but this time early in the morning, at precisely 4:37 am. So will there be as many people at the Place du Forum in Daix? Not so sure — many will no doubt still be asleep…

Lastly, Astro Daix, an activity of the Daix APCSD association, offers themed evenings and observation sessions with visits to sites related to astronomy throughout the year, for small groups of 6 to 15 people.

Jacques Revon
