Éliane et Jean-Pierre Laffont released the following tribute to Jean-Francois Leroy.

Oh Captain ! Our Captain !

Dear Jean François, Jean Pierre and I have been your friends for 40 years, we were so young then, full of ideas, hope and ambition and with health that could withstand anything.. We could discuss photography all night and go to work in the morning without having had an hour of sleep. We did so many things together, photography festivals, books, shows. And in every corner of the planet. We also had some great laughs because you are the funniest friend I know, the most flamboyant too and the one with the biggest mouth!

You are the friend everyone should have, phenomenal, charismatic, spiritual, profound, curious, loyal, passionate and fascinating, you also have a great moral ethic and an immense sense of justice. You are the best, the greatest !

Jean François, you have changed the lives of thousands of photographers, including Jean Pierre. You are the first to have taken photojournalism out of the pages of newspapers and magazines and put it on walls, in churches, in convents, in the prisons of the city of Perpignan and I will always remember Jean-Pierre’s wonder and emotion when he saw his photos on those giant screens. Jean François, you changed the way people see the world and the way photographers see their work.

The world of photography without you is simply unimaginable. You are the captain, the lighthouse in the storm.

I wish I could light up the Eiffel Tower and tell you what a beautiful light you are and that will remain in our lives.

Eliane and Jean-Pierre

Archives – September 2, 2025

This is one of Visa pour l’Image’s most interesting exhibitions this year.

Its title:In the Shadow of White Flags.

The photographer: Sandra Calligaro.

She accompanied her photos with this text.

JJN

On August 15, 2021, thanks to the American withdrawal, the Taliban regained power in Afghanistan, twenty years after being driven out. Upon their return, a leaden pall fell over the country. The media were muzzled, girls were excluded from secondary education, and music was banned. Women were once again ordered to cover themselves from head to toe: in the cities, the veils of long black abayas billowed alongside electric blue chadris. Excluded from most workplaces and social gatherings, they were erased from the public sphere, locked away in their homes. This exclusion is all the more painful, unspeakable, for city dwellers whom the West had encouraged to emancipate themselves and see the world differently.

Faced with the gradual establishment of theocracy, I sought to document the tragic daily lives of women: their confinement, but also their resilience. I wanted to paint a portrait of a constrained society, adapting as best it can and trying to resist increasingly restrictive decrees.

Driven indoors, women nevertheless find ways to continue living despite the restrictions. Hidden from view, clandestine schools welcome thousands of young students. Although their presence in public spaces is limited, women are still allowed to work in a few sectors such as healthcare, art, or crafts—gray areas into which they are quickly plunging.

Through gestures that may seem trivial to us but which, in this context, reveal true courage, young girls continue to learn—in living rooms, in basements, or via online programs. They continue to groom themselves in beauty salons operating behind closed doors. And since public education is forbidden to them beyond the 5th grade, they turn to art classes—in these workshops, they sometimes rub shoulders with young men. They defy Taliban law, but not only that: they also oppose a deeply patriarchal and conservative society, where oppression is not limited to religion.

I present Afghanistan in half-tone , suspended between hope and melancholy. My photographic approach is intended to be intimate. I pay particular attention to interiors the last spaces of freedom for women. As a woman myself, I can cross the parda, the symbolic and physical curtain that separates the sexes, to access these enclosed spaces where female life subsists. Conversely, in photographs taken outside, in spaces reserved for men, the eye searches for women and struggles to find them: they have become a detail in the image.

Implicitly, I also evoke those who, during these twenty years of international intervention, grew up far from the cities, in rural areas where aid did not reach. The young Taliban fighters are mostly from this youth who remained on the margins of progress. Lacking schooling, they attended madrasas, the Quranic schools, and from adolescence onwards, were recruited for jihad. Did they even have a choice over their destiny?

Two worlds, two Afghanistans, crushed by more than forty years of deadly conflict, collide: the aborted dreams of some, the vanished hopes, coexist with the return to light of others. It is this complexity inherent to war, and which fractures societies that my work attempts to embrace.

Sandra Calligaro. June 2025

Archives – September 3, 2024

American photographer Karen Ballard presents photographs at this year’s Visa pour l’imagein a solo exhibition at Maison de la Catalanité from her long-term documentary project on Venice, California.

Venice, CA is a compelling and keen insider’s view of the iconic, quirky, bohemian California coastal town known as an artistic hub and a public beach for all. It’s a place where beauty, surf, wealth, and the harsh realities of today exist side-by-side. Over the last decade Venice has slowly evolved from a storied past to a colorful, complicated, and modern present.

The Los Angeles enclave was founded July 4 th, 1905 by conservationist and dreamer Abbot Kinney who won hundreds of acres of coastal marshland south of Santa Monica on a bet. His vision, a ‘Venice of America,’ was to create a cultured resort town, complete with canals and gondolas, and a Coney Island-like amusement park on a pier over the Pacific Ocean. Most of that is gone as the original pier burned down and few of the canals remain. To his credit, Kinney’s dream has long outlived those early years, and millions of people visit Venice Beach every year making it the number one tourist attraction ­­­­in Southern California after Disneyland.

Over the past decade, the tech boom with its accompanying wealth has led to gentrification. For some that new money has become a plague on the spirit of this gritty beach town where over 40,000 people live. A rapid surge in income inequality, sky-rocketing rent prices, and an oversized unhoused population made worse by the pandemic has flipped Venice on its head.

“I could not have predicted this project, shot over the last decade and a half, would coincide with its ongoing transition,” says Ballard, “the disparity and wealth that now exists in Venice, represents an increasing fact of life in America in the 21st century.”

As Venice continues to evolve, this body of work is a visual study with a nod to its past and a hint to its future.

In the fall of 1994, Ballard made her first trip of many, to Perpignan. She was fresh out of college with several newspaper internships behind her, and a life in photography ahead. Ballard said, “It is my great honor to return exactly thirty years later with a solo exhibition at Visa Pour L’image. I am thrilled!”

David Hume KennerlyPulitzer Prize winner

Presidential Scholar,

The University of Arizona

Karen Ballardis an award-winning photojournalist, portrait and movie/television still photographer based in Los Angeles. She has covered major stories at The White House, on Capitol Hill, and has worked around the world, including assignments in the Middle East, Asia, and Africa. Steven Spielberg, wanting a photographer with Ballard’s journalistic sensibilities, hired her as his unit photographer for Munich.Since then she has shot over 20 feature films, working with among others, Daniel Craig on the James Bond film Quantum of Solace,Tom Cruise on Jack Reacher, and Sylvester Stallone on Rambo and The Expendables. She has recently worked on HBO Max’s Hacks and the Apple TV’s The Morning Show. Ballard’s work is in the permanent collections of the Smithsonian American History Museum and the Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA). At seventeen Ballard first visited Venice Beach where she made pictures on that eye-opening trip and vowed to return. Twenty-five years later she made Venice her home and embarked on a long-term documentary project about her eclectic American neighborhood.

KAREN BALLARD: VENICE, CAAugust 31-Sept 15 th

Archives Yan Morvan attended Visa pour l’Image in Perpignan. He gave us these images and this text.

Thanks Yan!

JJN

We could describe Visa 2022 in songs… “Avec le temps”, ” la ballade des gens heureux”, a music: “Once upon a time in the West”, “Gunfight at O.K. Corral”… But like these hummed tunes so often unforgettable we would always wish to keep them alive.

Visa is the vintage party of a bygone era of photojournalism. An excellent vinyl record with grooves that have written the history of the world for the past thirty years.

The exhibitions show the same images as thirty years ago; wars, famines, disasters… To make it modern, we added a touch of ecology and the defense of nature. The scenography is non-existent, walls lcovered with images that follow one after the other… sometimes we could even confuse subjects and photographers…

The public is present there, attentive to deciphering the captions written very small in the labels that decipher the images.

Sometimes on a dare a large picture! But here we are not in Arles! What is important is meaning not decoration.

On stage the high priest Leroy officiates… he wobbles from one end of the stage to the other, exhausted with fatigue… his baby barely lets him sleep…

We sometimes run into known faces, less and less, alcohol and tobacco have decimated a living environment of precariousness and extinct glories.

Young photographers are still just as determined and enthusiastic, the newsrooms are eager for cheap new blood. This year we mainly speak German and American, the war in Ukraine has awakened the international photo services. Americans pay $600 a day of war, it’s the holy grail for photographers who beg appointments from the heads of the New York Times, Washington Post and Wall Street Journal…

Paris-Match The title partner of the great Visa years has abandoned the ship, too absorbed in the episodes of “upgrading” in the mergers of the industrial press.

Canon is still there, until when? SLR cameras are no longer sold! make way for hybrids…

The restaurant opposite the café de la poste has burned down! A criminal act it seems… Under the Alliot era, the city has been gentrified and cleaned up to attract more tourists; The gypsies, many of whom voted RN, have been pushed away from their historic neighborhoods to the outskirts of the city.

I find familiar faces – only here can I see them gathered… JF Leroy created a star that is gradually dying out – it shone with a thousand lights – revealed talents – promoted and revealed impossible stories – brought together characters from all over the planet sharing the same passion – The world of tomorrow will be merciless for these image-pioneering adventurers. We will not end with der Abschied, the sublime end of the song of the earth by Gustav Mahler.

Yan Morvan

Visa pour l’image – Perpignan 2022– August 27 to September 11, 2022

Archives – September 5, 2020

Director of Visa pour Image, Jean-François Leroy discusses the reasons to maintain the festival, between support for photojournalists and the desire not to give up. Of this particular edition, he remembers above all what is positive and the innovations, notably the exhibitions and online screenings which bring new visitors to Visa all over the world.

Did the situation of photojournalists during lockdown motivate the continuation of Visa pour Image 2020?

JFL: The situation for photographers, which was already precarious, has become catastrophic with the confinement. People who haven’t traveled for three months have had no income for that entire period. At the same time, newspaper assignments have dwindled with the collapse of the advertising market. I know a lot of photographers who are in very difficult situations.

Much of the program for this 32nd edition was built during the pandemic. How did you go about building it in this very special year?

JFL: When we started working on the program, we weren’t sure we could do this edit. We therefore focused on choosing more timeless exhibitions, such as those of Chloé Sharrock, Victor Moriyama, James Whitlow Delano, Ian Willms or Elena Chernyshova. Their photos could be shown next year if we hadn’t been able to open to the public this year. And we refocused on current affairs in our projections so as not to throw exhibitions in the trash. Work like Emilienne Malfato’s on Iraq could no longer be seen next year.

The Covid-19 occupies an essential place in this 2020 edition. Have you received a lot of proposals?

JFL: Countless. Because this is the first time that the same event has affected all countries, all peoples, all regimes. With the Covid, photographers from all over the world have worked on the same subject. So inevitably there was a plethora of offers.

Was it difficult to choose between the proposals on this subject?

JFL: No. When you see the work of Peter Turnley, there is such empathy, such humanism in his photos, that it was easy to make up my mind. In addition, his work takes place in New York, one of the most important infectious hotspots in the United States. Empty Time Square is something I never imagined seeing in my life. We also wanted to take a world tour of the pandemic, with the Pandemic (s) exhibition in which we wanted to show the differences in views on similar events. Moreover, during the screening scheduled for Saturday, we will have a 13-minute block that will really tell the story of the epidemic around the world, notably through India, Colombia and Peru.

“I can’t do an exhibition every year on AIDS, on #MeToo, on tuberculosis in Eastern countries or on Ebola and measles in Africa. It’s in the projections. ” Jean-François Leroy

Have public subsidies to the festival been maintained in their entirety? Is the financial balance threatened by the defection of certain private partners?

JFL: The Ministry of Culture gave us an exceptional grant. We have lost some private partners, but also have obtained others, such as Orange or Google. All this made has made it possible to catch up with the defection of the former. Roughly speaking, we have the same budget as last year.

After three days of the festival, do you already have an idea of ​​the attendance?

JFL:Not really. Saturday and Sunday were only 20% less than the first weekend of last year. Yesterday we had a bad day because it was back to school. But I can’t answer a question like that after three days. We have to wait until the end of the festival to have real figures.

In the coming years, will festival-goers be able to find exhibitions and screenings online again?

JFL: Yes. This will allow us to reach an audience that does not usually come to Perpignan. For example, I spotted a funny thing last week: we have a lot of entries coming from Indonesia. I don’t know why, but there has been a spike in registrations from this country.

Are you not afraid that with this technical possibility, Perpignan will lose festival-goers?

JFL: Not at all. What people love about Visa is that we touch each other, kiss, drink shots, chat. A projection at Campo Santo, with a 24-meter screen, and the same projection on a tablet, does not have the same value. There isn’t the same magic and I think everyone is going to be anxious to find it again.

Without the big evening screenings at Campo Santo, did it make sense to maintain Visa 2020?

JFL: I think so. When you look at everything that has been canceled, I’m glad we exist this year. A reporter told me, “It’s not as glittering a Visa as it usually is, but it’s a Visa anyway. This is what I remember. I don’t feel like we’re having half a festival.

Does the future of Visa pour Image necessarily lie in Perpignan? Touches with Barcelona were mentioned here and there …

JFL: Fake news! I had touches with French cities but I never had a single touch or contact with Barcelona. Coming back to Perpignan, as long as I don’t screw up, I don’t see why I would change. I have teams that have been there for 32 years and I have great places. My only red line is my editorial independence.

Julien Francois and Audrey Duquenne

Jeoffrey Guillemard : Southern Border

“The US border begins in southern Mexico.” This is how Central American migrants talk of their journey to reach the American dream. Everything begins at the border of Mexico and Guatemala on makeshift rafts launched on the Suchiate River. They must then walk for days before venturing on “La Bestia” (The Beast), the famous freight train that crosses the country. Alone or in a caravan, despite the length of the journey and the many dangers, thousands of migrants from Honduras, El Salvador and Guatemala take this route every day to escape the gangs and violence that are afflicting their respective countries. They lose their money, their dignity and sometimes even life.

This long-running reportage began with the inauguration of US President Donald Trump in 2017.

https://loeildelaphotographie.com/en/arc.content:
Archives – September 8, 2017

The International Festival of Photojournalism in Perpignan once again takes its visitors on a world tour, offering a fresh look at the state of the planet beyond the narrative clichés often made necessary by the urgent need to document.

In the introduction to his exhibition at Hotel Pams in Perpignan, entitled Tumulte et solitude en Afrique[Turmoil and Solitude in Africa], Marco Longari writes: “A news image is a subject onto itself; the emergency conditions in which we operate force us to concentrate information rather than dilute it over multiple images. […] Information, as it is presented to the public, is charged with meaning: the suggestiveness of an image may foster understanding, or else be yet another barrier, presenting the faraway, distracted, detached viewer with an added enigma.”

The AFP’s photographer-in-chief for Africa, Marco Longari, refuses to talk about a single Africa mired in political crises. His responsibility as a photographer, he says, lies in the nuance, with the hope that the public will be capable of discerning it and constructing their own image of the world. While Longari talks about urgency in the context of Africa, Visa pour l’Image embodies this demand in a broader sense, specifically in this 2017 edition.

Among the exhibiting photographers rare are those who have not worked for years on end in the country or region they are examining from all angles—whether violent, ephemeral, or ordinary. At the Couvent des Minimes, in an exhibition entitled Le Venezuela au bord du gouffre [Venezuela on the Edge of the Abyss], Meridith Kohut delves into the country’s collapse, from the empty supermarkets, which have made the headlines, to psychiatric hospitals, invisible spaces, which, however, shouts out what the rest of the population, for better or worse, is holding back: “I’m not mad, I’m hungry,” says a female patient, blushing.

In an adjacent room, an exhibition surveys the work of Laurent Van der Stockt, who closely followed the battle for Mosul in Iraq and watched the Islamic State being pushed back, one frontline at a time, at the cost of enormous losses and countless refugees. The fighters are not anonymous: we know their names, we see them again and again, months apart; our hearts break when we read they are dead and that we will no longer follow the battle through their eyes. And when we see images of civilians applauding their liberators, we share the crowd’s emotions.

The same is true of another exhibition, shown a little further on:Ukraine: d’une guerre à l’autre[Ukraine: From One War to the Next] Rafael Yaghobzadeh has covered multiple points of view and varied perspectives since 2014 in order to report on the conflict in all its day-to-day complexity. The time invested in documenting a place allows the photographer to tell a multifaceted story. And this is the takeaway from this year’s Visa, with its diversity of geographies and subject matters.

And if the exhibitions are not evidence enough, Visa is also an opportunity for twelve other photographers to announce the creation of a collective structure called MAPS, which promotes perseverance and transparency. Who are its members? Alessandro Penso, Cédric Gerbehaye, Christian Lutz, Dominic Nahr, Gaël Turine, Hannah Reyes Morales, John Trotter, John Vink, Justyna Mielnikiewicz, Massimo Berruti, Matthieu Gafsou, and Simona Ghizzoni are announcing upcoming group and multidisciplinary projects. This is yet another promise in the service of information that is time-consuming to gather and impart.

Laurence CornetLaurence Cornet is a journalist and exhibition curator.

Je n’ai jamais eu à m’inquiéter d’avoir un appareil photo avec moi, j’avais tous mes appareils photo avec moi. « J’habite ici. » Je ne l’ai jamais pris pour acquis quand je rentrais de pays exotiques; il était toujours là à m’attendre. From September 3rd 2026 to September 19th 2027, to mark the Bicentenary of Photography, the LUX Network is rolling out a packed programme of events in Paris and across the country. From September 2026 and throughout 2027, a tour of France in a mobile analogue photography laboratory caravan will offer a unique, participatory and immersive artistic experience entitled LUX TOUR. The travelling caravan, which will be launched in Paris on Thursday September 3rd, will stop off at each of the network’s member festivals and fairs across France. Conceived as a symbol of the circulation of works, ideas and audiences, this exceptional initiative will connect different regions and highlight the richness of a network that works year-round to promote and showcase photography, whilst playing an essential role in providing access to culture and visual literacy.

The caravan will offer visitors a unique experience, thanks to the ‘À l’origine du Cœur’ project led by the Trigone Collective. The installation enables participants to take a photograph based on their heartbeat. Visitors are invited to enter the darkroom to take a photograph using their own heartbeat, via a process that captures cardiac activity. Once developed, the photographs are digitised and then printed to be given to the visitors. Each print is unique and represents a heartbeat at that precise moment in their lives.

For this tour across France, the LUX Network has chosen a 100 per cent electric BMW vehicle, the BMW iX3, in line with its eco-responsibility charter and its commitment to more sustainable mobility. The BMW iX3 offers more sustainable mobility with zero emissions during use; it tows the caravan and also supplies the energy needed to power it, enabling the travelling studio to operate freely as it moves from one stop to the next and meets new people. The partnership with BMW is part of this shared drive to encourage access to culture, visual literacy and support for contemporary creativity.

https://loeildelaphotographie.com/en/lon.content:
A 3-day photowalk, suitable for photographers of all levels will be held in London on the 9th, 10th and 11th October 2026.

Guided by the visual language of Giacomo Brunelli’s “Eternal London” (commissioned by The Photographers’ Gallery and published by Dewi Lewis Publishing), you’ll explore the very streets that shaped this body of work.

This intensive 3-day workshop offers photographers of all skill levels a unique opportunity to enhance their street photography practice.

The workshop will focus on developing crucial skills for aspiring and established photographers alike.

  • Project Development: Learn how to initiate and cultivate personal photography projects from concept to completion.
  • Composition and Moment Capture: Refine your visual acumen to identify compelling compositions and effectively capture engaging moments, even with unfamiliar subjects.
  • Critical Evaluation and Editing: Develop a discerning eye for critically assessing, editing, and refining your photographic output to strengthen your artistic vision.
  • Portfolio Building: Construct a powerful portfolio that authentically showcases your individual style and artistic perspective.
  • Visual Storytelling: Understand the principles of photography as a medium for impactful storytelling.
  • Pathways to Publishing: Gain insights into the diverse avenues for photographic publishing, from independent self-publishing to engaging with established publishing house.

Dates

Friday 9th October 2026

Saturday 10th October 2026

Sunday 11th October 2026

-Time: 10:00 AM – 3:00 PM each day (includes Photowalk and review sessions)

What to bring

-Your camera

– A portfolio of 15-30 images

Meeting Point

-Waterloo Station (Waterloo Rd, London SE1 8SW)

Locations

-The workshop will be held in Central London, we will be exploring different areas such as Hyde Park, St.James’s, Piccadilly and along the River Thames.

Fee £495

https://loeildelaphotographie.com/en/cal.content:
This coming November, the town of Belfort (France) is organising the 9th edition of Mois de la Photo, an event dedicated to contemporary photography. Through this event, it reaffirms its commitment to artistic creation, to supporting professional photographers and to promoting their work.

At the same time, the Entrevues Belfort International Film Festival, organised by the Cinémas d’Aujourd’hui association, will take place from November 16th to 22 2026 at the Kinepolis cinema in Belfort. Dedicated to showcasing contemporary cinema and emerging talent, the festival shares with Mois de la Photo a common desire to promote today’s artistic expressions.

Building on these shared ambitions, the Mois de la Photo and the Entrevues Festival are joining forces for the third consecutive year to present a photography prize, aimed at professional photographers and to artists and authors.

The winner will be awarded a paid solo exhibition, to be held in November 2026 as part of the Mois de la Photo and the Entrevues Festival, as well as enhanced visibility amongst the audiences of both events.

This year, the competition echoes the Entrevues Festival’s ‘Transversale’ programme, centred on the theme of ‘Game’.

A universal phenomenon, games transcends ages, cultures and societies, as a space for learning, experimentation and freedom, it allows us to invent rules, follow them or subvert them. Beyond mere entertainment, it reveals social dynamics, power relations and individual or collective imaginations. In both cinema and photography, games also fuel the creative act: the interplay of the gaze, light and framing, straddling the line between fiction and reality. We invite photographers to offer a personal and contemporary take on this theme.

To apply, simply complete the online form by midnight on 8 September 2026.

https://loeildelaphotographie.com/en/the.content:
Sandrine Arons : What the image does not show

For Sandrine Arons, the true subject of photography begins precisely where the visible ends.

Her images do not document reality: they put it to the test. They question what we think we see, what we have forgotten to look at, and what an image sometimes reveals only in retrospect. For her, photography is less about capturing than exploring. A face, a body, a landscape, an object become entry points into a more interior reality, shaped by memory, sensations, absences and fragments of identity. This approach is anything but accidental. Sandrine Arons’ gaze has been shaped at the intersection of several territories photography, literature, psychology and painting and this permeability runs through her entire practice. Magritte, Caravaggio and Frida Kahlo stand alongside Sally Mann, Sophie Calle, Dorothea Lange and Richard Avedon in a pantheon that already says much about the way she conceives the image: not as a transparent window onto the world, but as a space of displacement, uncertainty and interpretation. In her series, reality splits and doubles. Frontiers emerged from her travels and her multicultural experience, without initially being conceived as a project about identity. Only later did she recognize a recurring motif within her own images: that of borders, both geographical and psychological, and their inability to remain completely impermeable. With Multiplicity, the process is reversed. The concept comes before the image: several “selves” — woman, mother, wife, daughter must coexist within a single photographic space. Not as a digital construction, but as a physical manifestation of this inner coexistence. This desire to make the invisible visible finds its most intimate expression in her relationship to memory. The portrait she took of her father after his death becomes, for her, a threshold image, suspended between a before and an after. As for the photographs she made over nearly seven years of her mother, who was living with a degenerative disease, they raise an altogether more vertiginous question: can disappearance be photographed without betraying it? These images, still kept outside the exhibition space, bear witness to a practice willing to look where looking becomes difficult. Her attachment to black and white stems from the same imperative. Far from being an aesthetic form of nostalgia, it allows her to strip away whatever might distract the eye. To remove color in order to reach a form of essence. To silence the setting so that we can listen to what the image says otherwise. “What is real?” she asks. What was experienced? What we remember? Or what photography reveals to us when we look at it again? Perhaps it is within this gap that Sandrine Arons’ territory lies. Between the image and what it sets in motion. Between reality and its memory. Between what we look at and what, suddenly, looks back at us. Her photography does not necessarily seek to provide answers. It prefers to leave a crack. And it is through that crack that something gets through.

Website : www.sandrinearons.com

Instagram:@sandrinearons

Your first photographic trigger?Sandrine Arons: I think the initial click happened in my brain. Ever since I was a child, I’ve been mentally capturing images, like moments frozen in my mind. It’s almost as if a shutter were going off inside my head. When I finally got my first “real” camera, it became an extension of my mind: I could actually press the shutter and freeze those moments. But never enough! Even today, I walk around with that little shutter in my head, and I regret the moments I’ve missed because I didn’t have my camera with me or didn’t react quickly enough.

A photographic memory from your childhood?Sandrine Arons: One memory related to photography that comes back to me is about the father of my childhood best friend, when I was six or seven. He had a darkroom at home, and I remember seeing him going in and out completely naked. I imagine he was developing his photographs naked. I remember the photographs hanging to dry on a line. It’s a slightly bizarre memory, but that’s also how I discovered that you could develop your own photographs at home.

The camera of your childhood?Sandrine Arons: A Polaroid instant camera, and then a Vivitar V2000, which I bought when I was 18.

The one you use today?Sandrine Arons: Sony A7RIV, Sony 6700, SEMFLEX TLR (from the 1950s), Fuji Instant, and my iPhone.

The man or woman of the image who inspired you?Sandrine Arons: It’s not just one person. I’ve drawn a lot of inspiration from painters and from their own ways of treating the image. So, for me, it would be Magritte, Caravaggio and Frida Kahlo, for example. In photography, Sally Mann, Sophie Calle, Annie Leibovitz, Dorothea Lange, Pedro Meyer, Richard Avedon, and many others.

The image you wish you had taken?Sandrine Arons:Candy Cigarette by Sally Mann or Lunch Atop a Skyscraper by Charles Clyde Ebbets.

The one that moved you the most?Sandrine Arons: There isn’t one particular image, but I would say several photographs taken during the liberation of the concentration camps. They are powerful and deeply affecting images that immediately trigger complex emotions in me. I would say they are the ones that have left the deepest mark on me.

And the one that made you angry?Sandrine Arons: Perhaps the same ones I mentioned above. But more recently, I would also say the photographs showing ICE agents in the United States hitting people, arresting them and placing them in detention, as well as the faces of the children watching all this, terrified. They immediately provoke feelings of anger, sadness, frustration and shock in me. And fortunately, these images exist as evidence. I strongly believe in photography as a witness.

Which photograph changed the world?Sandrine Arons: Again, I can’t think of a single photograph, but rather several. Photographs of wars, photographs of the Earth seen from space.

And which photograph changed your world?Sandrine Arons: The photograph I took of my father, who had just died. It was a farewell, a final image to preserve a trace of him at the moment of his departure. The beginning of another life. A photograph on the boundary between before and after… for him and for me.

A key image in your personal pantheon?Sandrine Arons: I would say it’s a black-and-white photograph of my son, about to run under a jet of water, one summer in Morocco. It was the first photograph I ever exhibited, and it won the exhibition’s grand prize. To me, it was a sign that I had found my way back on the right path.

What interests you most in an image?Sandrine Arons: Light, emotions, details. I tend to look for those little details that aren’t immediately perceptible.

What details do you look for in a face, a landscape or an object?Sandrine Arons: In a face, the eyes and the lips. What are they communicating? In a landscape, shapes. In an object, precision.

Elliott Erwitt said: “Color is descriptive. Black and white is interpretive.” Do you agree?Sandrine Arons: I think black and white reveals the essence of a world, a place, a person, etc. In my eyes, color can distract the gaze from the essence. It represents what we see with our eyes, but is what we see really real? It’s a complex question for me. I’m not sure I consider black and white more interpretive or more artistic. I see it more as a liberation from everything that so often covers or obscures reality. Black and white eliminates the superfluous in order to get to the essential. So, what is real? I think that’s the real question. For me, reality is closer to black and white than to color. Personally, when I want to express a deep emotion, or reveal something intimate, personal and true about myself or someone else, I generally choose to use black and white.

Can technique sometimes take precedence over emotion in photography?Sandrine Arons: Yes, it can happen, but it shouldn’t. I have to be careful about that myself, especially when I photograph professional portraits for clients. I can let myself be guided by technique because clients expect technically correct portraits. It succeeds when technique and emotion come together. On the other hand, when I photograph for myself, I think less about technique. I allow myself to go against what I’ve learned, not to necessarily follow the rules… and above all, to play… to let the subject guide me rather than guiding the subject. For me, technique remains an essential foundation. Without knowing the basic rules of photography or knowing how to use my camera, I would inevitably be more limited in what I can create and express. So technique also helps me reveal emotion like a good psychologist.

Is beauty in photography, for you, purely aesthetic?Sandrine Arons: No. There are sad or violent photographs that I find beautiful. For example, photographs of cities devastated by war or bombings. I can find beauty in a tree that has remained standing amid the ruins, in the light of a clear sky after the destruction, or in an abandoned stuffed animal. The tragic can be beautiful, and beauty can be tragic.

What elements can make silence visible in a photograph?Sandrine Arons: I return to what I said in the previous question. A tree, a doll, any object that seems out of place. A gaze, too. Curiously, I also find that movement in a photograph can make the silence it breaks even more visible. If I see a photograph of a turbulent sea, with waves crashing, my mind immediately wants to calm it down, to transform it into a still and silent sea. In a way, all that visual noise creates a need for silence in me. So the image becomes silent.

Does the uniqueness of a photograph come from the moment or from the staging?Sandrine Arons: I think it can be both.

Can a photograph be truer than reality?Sandrine Arons: At least in terms of what it communicates, I would say YES. In life, many things escape us. A photograph captures what is often invisible in our everyday lives. Sometimes, a photograph I’ve taken reveals something I didn’t see at the time I took it. So, what is real: my experience of the moment, or what the photograph shows?

Can a photograph change our perception of an event?Sandrine Arons: Yes, if we are open to changing the way we see things.

Is photography a testimony or a form of manipulation?Sandrine Arons: I think it can be both. Besides, a testimony itself can be a source of manipulation… for good or for bad.

What makes a good photograph?Sandrine Arons: I think it’s different for everyone. For me, a good photograph is one that makes me want to stop and look at it longer. It’s a photograph that triggers something visceral in me. It can make me smile, cry or laugh. It often comes back to me and makes me want to see it again and again. A good photograph communicates with me and seeks to develop a relationship with me over time.

In your opinion, what quality is essential to being a good photographer?Sandrine Arons: Open-mindedness, patience, empathy, curiosity, courage…

How do you choose your projects?Sandrine Arons: Sometimes I embark on a project because I feel the need to express something that is important to me. Sometimes projects simply come along on their own, because I’m having fun, experimenting, and it’s as if the project comes looking for me. Sometimes, too, I’m inspired by other forms of art or by other artists. Writers and literature in general often give me ideas for projects. I also think that some projects mature somewhere inside me, in my mind or in my body, until the moment comes when they need to be born.

How would you describe your creative process?Sandrine Arons: In one word: complicated. It really depends on the project. I like exploring different ways of making photographs, so my approach varies considerably. I love pure or direct photography, experimental photography, but I also enjoy creating images with Photoshop, etc. If I have something very specific in mind, such as a particular style of portrait, I’ll first do some research, then experiment in my studio. For a broader project, I tend to let the idea or emotion live inside me for a while and wait for the subject to come to me. For example, with my Frontiers series, I had absolutely no intention of making a project around this theme. It emerged naturally through my travel photographs and my desire to visually express what it felt like to be multicultural. I never thought, “I’m going to make a project about my multiculturalism.” I simply noticed something recurring in my images and listened to what they were telling me. It’s almost a kind of stream-of-consciousness photography. With Multiplicity, it was different. There, I knew from the beginning what I wanted to explore: what it means to be a mother, wife, woman, daughter, etc., and all the confusion, frustration, anger, sadness, but also the ecstasy that this can bring. So I had the idea, but then I had to find a way to show it. I chose to bring these different roles, these different “selves,” into a single photograph. It was important to me that they all actually exist within the same image, because that felt closer to what I was experiencing. I didn’t want to add them later in Photoshop or create double or triple exposures. So I created a space and set aside days to work at home without interruption, and I simply went for it. And sometimes a series begins with just one image, because I’m bored or testing something. Then I think, “Oh, I like this,” and I continue. That’s exactly what happened with my Myself AS… series. So yes, I would say my creative process changes considerably depending on the project.

A forthcoming project that is particularly close to your heart?Sandrine Arons: I always have several projects in mind at the same time, but there is one that has been with me for a long time: a project about my mother and her life after being diagnosed with a degenerative disease. I took care of her for almost seven years and photographed all the years during which her condition deteriorated, until her death a few years ago. Among my other projects, I often return to these photographs, write about them, and tell myself that one day I will have to share them. I think I haven’t done so yet for several reasons, particularly because I wonder how the people who knew her, especially her friends, would react to seeing photographs of her in such a fragile state. They are very personal images that show the reality of this disease. At the same time, we had decided together, at the beginning of her diagnosis, that I would photograph her over the years. For her too, it was important to document this period.

The person you would like to photograph?Sandrine Arons: My father, if he were still alive.

The person you would like to be photographed by?Sandrine Arons: I don’t like being photographed anymore. But if I had to be photigraphed, I would want a beautiful black-and-white portrait by Yousuf Karsh or Annie Leibovitz.

An essential photography book? One that inspires you?Sandrine Arons: More recently, for me, A World History of Women Photographers by Luce Lebart and Marie Robert.

What is the last photograph you took?Sandrine Arons: A photograph of Jesus on the large cross That is Place Giral, in front of the Promenade du Peyrou in Montpellier, in the evening during a storm.

On social media, are you more Instagram, Facebook or TikTok — and why?Sandrine Arons: For photographs, definitely Instagram. It’s the best way to share my photographs (I don’t do it enough), and especially, for me, to discover other photographers.

What has changed in photography since the rise of social media?Sandrine Arons: I think we have access to many more projects by other photographers, and it allows us to discover, exchange and communicate with artists we probably never would have known otherwise. There are some truly beautiful photographs on social media, and it often pushes me to create differently, for better or worse. It’s also a good way to find courses, workshops or exhibitions. I also think it has given photography a real boost and that people now see photography more as an art form. But at the same time, sometimes it feels as though everyone wants to become a photographer. The problem is that it takes an enormous amount of time. Sometimes it feels like we spend more time posting and scrolling than creating. And when we have other things to do alongside it, it’s difficult to keep our accounts up to date. Honestly, I have quite an ambivalent relationship with social media… as an artist, as a mother, as a woman.

One Instagram account you absolutely have to follow?Sandrine Arons: There are too many… not just one. You should follow the artists whose work catches your attention at first glance — the ones that “stop you in your tracks.”

What is your view on AI?Sandrine Arons: I have quite a mixed opinion about AI. It’s like any new technology: we need to learn how to master it and use it appropriately.

In photography, I think AI can be “used” to create, but it shouldn’t itself be the source of creation. I find that images entirely generated by AI lack essence, aura. They can be decorative, but I find them uninteresting. I think young people recognize that immediately. My 17-year-old son instantly recognizes AI-generated images and hates them. That reassures me.

Color or black and white?Sandrine Arons: Both.

Natural light or artificial light?Sandrine Arons: Both, but I prefer artificial light for portraits.

Which city seems the most photogenic to you?Sandrine Arons: Any city in Morocco. And then Paris and New York.

The city, country or culture you dream of discovering?Sandrine Arons: Vietnam.

The place you never tire of?Sandrine Arons: Morocco.

The image that represents the current state of the world for you?Sandrine Arons: The recent photograph by Maximilien Lamy of a couple sitting on the beach under their parasol, watching the fires in front of them.

In your opinion, what is missing from the world today?Sandrine Arons: Pragmatism, depth and the courage to be oneself.

If God existed, would you ask him to pose for you, or would you opt for a selfie with him?Sandrine Arons: If God existed, he would be everywhere, in everything. So I have already taken many photographs of God: in a landscape, a portrait, a flower, a cloud. In that case, I’m ultimately only photographing God, and every selfie would be God because God would also be within me.

Your favorite drug?Sandrine Arons: The one that makes me rediscover the world with fresh eyes and doesn’t kill me. These days, mostly travel.

Your best way to disconnect?Sandrine Arons: Reading. Walking. Music. Travel.

Your latest folly?Sandrine Arons: I’m too sensible. I don’t know.

Your greatest professional extravagance?Sandrine Arons: The amount of money I spend on everything related to photography.

The job you would never have wanted to do?Sandrine Arons: Plumber.

Which question leaves you most at a loss?Sandrine Arons: “Where are you from?” I never know how to answer.

The last thing you did for the first time?Sandrine Arons: I switched from a gasoline-powered car to an electric one.

Your greatest regret?Sandrine Arons: Not having photographed my father more while he was alive.

If you had to start all over again?Sandrine Arons: I would start photography at a younger age.

If I could organize your ideal dinner, who would be sitting around the table?Sandrine Arons: My father and my son, who never had the chance to meet.

What would you like people to say about you… afterwards?Sandrine Arons: That I existed and that I passed on something useful to them.

The one thing people absolutely need to know about you?Sandrine Arons: They need to know that I’m very shy and that I find it difficult to express myself verbally when I don’t know someone well. What I show others doesn’t always reflect everything that is happening inside me. There is much more beneath the surface. And I don’t know how to pretend.

One last word?

]Life is not stable, and you have to be ready to change direction, whether for a few moments or a few years, But you always have to stay centered and listen to yourself.

The J. Paul Getty Museumpresents “Every Minute Is History: Five Views of Los Angeles”. Featuring works by five photographers – Laura Aguilar, Reynaldo Rivera, George Rodriguez, Patssi Valdez, and Ricardo Valverde – this exhibition explores how these artists expanded the understanding of the built environment and cultural landscape of Los Angeles, along with the representations of Latino/a communities in the city during the second half of the 20th century.

“Through their unique visions, these photographers have challenged conventional narratives and broadened the ways Latino/a lives are represented,” said Timothy Potts, Maria Hummer-Tuttle and Robert Tuttle Director of the J. Paul Getty Museum. “Their work documents histories that have often been overlooked, while also exploring deeply personal themes of identity, belonging, and creative expression.”

Emerging during and after the Chicano Liberation Movement of the 1960s, the artists in the exhibition demonstrate the breadth of photographic practices that celebrated Latino/a and Chicano/a identities by blending documentary, conceptual, and experimental approaches to create enduring records of Los Angeles’s cultural and physical landscapes.

George Rodriguez (American, born 1937) documented both celebrity culture and the collective political struggles of Mexican Americans during the Chicano Movement. His photographs capture pivotal moments in Los Angeles history, including the Sunset Strip Riots, the United Farm Workers movement, and subsequent periods of social unrest, creating a powerful visual record of civic activism and cultural change.

Ricardo Valverde (American, 1946–1998) used photography to chronicle his family, friends, and the East Los Angeles community in which he lived. While working for the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power, he photographed daily life throughout the city. In the final decade of his career, Valverde experimented with photographic materials, revisiting older negatives and altering prints with pigment and incised marks to create richly textured and increasingly abstract images.

Laura Aguilar (American, 1959–2018) became renowned for her compassionate portraits of queer communities and for her vulnerable self-portraits. After studying at East Los Angeles College, Aguilar created intimate photographs that explored identity, visibility, and belonging, often positioning her own body within the landscapes of the American Southwest.

Reynaldo Rivera (American, born 1964 in Mexico) documented the vibrant underground music, nightlife, and drag performance scenes of Los Angeles during the 1980s and 1990s. His photographs capture spaces where conventional boundaries of gender, class, and sexuality dissolved, preserving communities that flourished outside mainstream visibility.

Patssi Valdez (American, born 1951), widely recognized as a co-founder of the influential artist collective ASCO, turned her attention in the mid-1980s to highly personal studio-based photography and documentations of performances. Her work often centered on friends and collaborators, including those involved in the paper fashion shows organized by Self Help Graphics & Art, the community arts center in East Los Angeles that began staging annual Day of the Dead festivities in 1982.

“This exhibition brings together a number of important artists working in Los Angeles during the second half of the twentieth century whose photographs have helped to shape and expand our understanding of this city and whose subject matter also often addressed Latino/a and Chicano/a culture, histories, and artistic aspirations,” says associate curator, Arpad Kovacs. “This exhibition is an opportunity for the Museum to celebrate recent acquisitions and reiterate our commitment to better understand and represent our local communities through our collection.”

“Every Minute Is History: Five Views of Los Angeles” is curated by Arpad Kovacs, associate curator in the Department of Photographs, and is presented in conjunction with “Instante/revelación: Moments in Mexican Photography,” which explores the rich tapestry of cultural and artistic dialogues that have shaped Mexico’s photographic history.

The Print Center presents Ron Tarver: The Long Ride Home, Black Cowboys in America, an exhibition that reveals the depth, breadth, beauty and visual poetry of Black cowboys throughout America. Until recently, popular culture had not recognized the vital Black contribution to our national stories of “The American West.” The Long Ride Home offers a contemporary counter-narrative to the traditional whitewashed myths. Tarver’s insightful photographs of Black Western heritage affirm a thriving culture of Black-owned ranches, rodeos, parades, inner-city cowboys and retired cowhands, from rural ranches to big city riding clubs – many in Philadelphia.

Growing up in Oklahoma, Tarver was surrounded by a vibrant Black cowboy culture. When he moved to Philadelphia in 1983, he found that this culture was virtually unknown on the East Coast. This revelation inspired a photo series for The Philadelphia Inquirer that began in 1992 and eventually became a cover story for their Sunday Magazine. An outpouring of reader support spurred the series on. He’s been correcting the American cowboy narrative with his photographs ever since. Set against the recent ascent of Black Western culture and the nation’s Semiquincentennial, Tarver’s color photographs celebrate this heritage as a foundational part of American history and contemporary culture. All shot in the 1990s, these 40 images bear witness to the lived experiences of Black cowboys and cowgirls across the U.S.

Tarver is a Pulitzer Prize, Pew Fellowship and Guggenheim Fellowship-winning photographer. For 32 years, he worked as a photojournalist for The Philadelphia Inquirer, and his striking images have been widely exhibited nationally and internationally. His award-winning book, The Long Ride Home: BlackCowboys in America (George F. Thompson Publishing, 2024), has received significant critical and popular acclaim – the first printing sold out within 30 days of its release.

His dedication to photographing Black cowboys has inspired artists, filmmakers and photographers like Ivan McClellan, who calls Tarver the “North Star as far as where the work can go.”

“This project has allowed me to reflect on my personal heritage of growing up in the West,” says Tarver. “While I do not consider myself a cowboy, I have a deep respect and admiration for those in the Black community who live out their western heritage every day. It is my hope that this exhibition affirms today’s thriving culture of Black-owned ranches, rodeo operations and inner-city cowboys, and inspires further conversation about what it means to be a cowboy—as well as what it means to be an American.

“Cowboys come in many colors. It’s time Black cowboys get their due.”

“Serving as the fiscal sponsor for this award-winning book and exhibition project has been an incredibly rewarding experience. The Print Center is guided by a dedication to supporting artists, and seeing Tarver’s work receive the recognition and accolades it deserves, especially after so much time, is deeply gratifying. We are thrilled to share this work in Philadelphia, as well as to steward its travel around the country – sharing Tarver’s love letter to this culture with a wide audience.”

– Elizabeth Spungen, Executive Director

Ron Tarver (b.1957, Fort Gibson, OK; l. Elkins Park, PA), has a BA from Northeastern State University, Tahlequah, OK, and an MFA from the University of the Arts, Philadelphia, PA. He was a staff photojournalist at The Philadelphia Inquirer for 32 years, where he won a Pulitzer Prize and awards from World Press Photos, Society of Professional Journalists and National Press Photographers Association. Tarver has received Guggenheim Foundation, Independence Foundation, NEA and Pew Fellowships.

His work has been exhibited in numerous exhibitions nationally and internationally, including at The Print Center, Philadelphia. It is included in many collections, including the State Museum of Pennsylvania, Harrisburg; The Studio Museum in Harlem, New York, NY; Philadelphia Museum of Art; and Smithsonian American Art Museum, Washington, DC. Tarver’s work has been published in Ebony, Jet, Life, National Geographic, Newsweek, Sports Illustrated and Time, and has appeared online on Huffington Post and Hyperallergic. He co-authored We Were There: Voices of African American Veterans (2004), which accompanied a traveling exhibition that debuted at the National Constitution Center. His award-winning second book is The Long Ride Home: Black Cowboys in America (2024). Tarver is Associate Professor/Department Chair of Art, Swarthmore College, PA.

Una vez más este año, Arles se transformó en una vasta ciudad dedicada a la fotografía. Para la 57a edición de los Rencontres d’Arles, me fané a través de las exposiciones con el sentido de que, más que las imágenes, era nuestra forma de ver que se estaba poniendo a prueba. Del cuerpo a los animales, de la intimidad al trabajo, de la familia a las historias olvidadas, las obras que encontraron las mismas imágenes ¿estás pregunta?

Empiezo con Ming Smith y Lueur nomade, Presentada en la Église Sainte-Anne. El escenario da a las fotografías una presencia particular: creadas durante varias décadas, las imágenes entran en diálogo con la arquitectura histórica y parecen saltar en algún lugar entre la memoria, el movimiento y la música. Smith fotografías ciudades, encuentros, cuerpos y gestos con un enfoque notablemente libre, en el que el borrón, el color y el movimiento se vuelven casi material en sí mismos.

Esta atención a los detalles de la vida cotidiana también se puede encontrar en la obra de Rinko Kawauchi, cuya serie Aila se presenta en Animal de Modèle. 200 ans de photographie, comisariado por Nathalie Herschdorfer. Otro aspecto de su trabajo se puede ver en una exposición separada,De Nuestra Windows, Presentada con Tokuko Ushioda en Vague como parte de Arles Associé. La exposición explora la intimidad doméstica, la vida familiar y los gestos cotidianos. Perteneciendo a diferentes generaciones, los dos artistas observan la vida cotidiana con gran sensibilidad. Agradezco especialmente su capacidad de dar importancia a momentos que, tomados individualmente, pueden parecer casi inconsecuentes.

La mirada se vuelve mucho más directa en L’image cannibale, presentado en la Capilla de la Charité. La exposición se acerca a la fotografía como un medio que “devora” lo que representa. Entre las obras que más me impactaron fue Mélissa Boucher El Scrolling de Morales [faire défiler] (2024). Utilizando fotografía analógica, la artista fotografía imágenes tomadas de vídeos de transmisión con cámaras, post-pornografía y pornografía feminista. Aisla fragmentos de cuerpos y gestos perdidos dentro del flujo digital, transformándolos hasta que adquieran una apariencia casi espectral. Luego se coloca un panel reflectante de vidrio sobre las imágenes, confrontando a los espectadores con su propia posición como voyeurs.

En La Mécanique générale, Un animal de Modèle. 200 ans de photographie extiende esta reflexión a la forma en que miramos a los animales. En lugar de seguir una estructura cronológica, la exposición se organiza alrededor de siete perspectivas fotográficas: la mirada anatómica, que observa y clasifica; la mirada performativa, que registra las hazañas animales; la mirada afectiva, centrada en los animales domésticos; la mirada fascinada, que celebra su belleza; la mirada ética, que hace visible su explotación; la mirada estética, que explora sus formas de ficción

Lo que más me interesa aquí es que la exposición, en última instancia, dice tanto sobre nosotros como sobre los animales. Si fotografiamos a un animal para estudiar, amar, admirar, explotar o proteger, revela nuestra propia posición en relación con el mundo viviente. Doscientos años de fotografía nos permiten rastrear la evolución de nuestra relación con los animales, pero también las formas cambiantes en que nos posicionamos en relación con ellos.

También he descubierto 5bis, la exposición de Charlotte Gainsbourg explorando su relación con su hogar familiar en la rue de Verneuil en París y el legado dejado por su padre, Serge Gainsbourg. A través de fotografías, objetos y fragmentos de memoria, construye una narrativa íntima alrededor de un lugar que se ha convertido en legendario. Me atrajo a la naturaleza profundamente personal del proyecto: la casa no es simplemente un entorno, sino que se convierte en casi un personaje a su derecha, lleno de recuerdos y ausencia.

Con Harry Gruyaert Un sentido del lugar [Le sens du lieu], la fotografía vuelve a la ciudad y viaja. Presentada en la Capilla Saint-Martin du Méjan, la exposición reúne imágenes tomadas en ciudades tan variadas como Nueva York, París, Tokio, Moscú y Mumbai. Gruyaert no tiene tantos destinos documentados como construir paisajes fuera de color, forma y fragmentos de la vida urbana. Dentro de esta antigua capilla, el contraste entre la arquitectura y las fotografías de su cromo.

En el Control Terrestre, un antiguo sitio ferroviario, Vigilancia. Le travail sous tension particularly caught my attention. La exposición reúne archivos fotográficos relacionados con la electricidad, la industria y, sobre todo, la prevención de accidentes de trabajo. Detrás de imágenes monumentales de infraestructura eléctrica, los trabajadores emergen gradualmente, junto con gestos técnicos y los peligros invisibles asociados a sus trabajos. Encontré el proyecto particularmente interesante porque demuestra cómo una fotografía aparentemente documental también puede convertirse en una herramienta para la memoria y la rendición de cuentas.

Por último, en la Fondation Manuel Rivera-Ortiz, Vengan juntos. reúne a artistas que exploran diferentes formas de conexión: familia, solidaridad, separación, transmisión, encuentros y aislamiento. Entre los proyectos que se encuentran, Andi Gáldi Vinkó’s Siento haberle dado a luz pero ahora estoy de vuelta. (2016–2022) especialmente resonó conmigo. Dibujo por su propia experiencia de maternidad, la artista fotografía las transformaciones corporales, el agotamiento, los niños y las convulsiones de la vida cotidiana, cuestionando el lugar de una mujer artista después de dar a luz.

Agradezco la forma en que Gáldi Vinkó se niega a presentar la maternidad como una experiencia totalmente alegre o totalmente difícil. En cambio, revela sus contradicciones: amor y agotamiento, alegría y pérdida de libertad, experiencia de ser madre y necesidad de recuperar su lugar como artista. Es precisamente esta honestidad que hace que el proyecto se sienta profundamente personal y universal.

Termino mi visita con Lee Shulman y Omar Victor Diop El Proyecto Anónimo – Estando allí. Los artistas intervienen en las fotografías familiares estadounidenses de los años 50 y 1960, introduciendo una presencia negra en escenas donde la historia y la segregación racial habían hecho imposible tal presencia. Estas escenas aparentemente ordinarias se convierten en imágenes alternativas, revelando todo lo que las fotografías pueden salir fuera del marco. Encontré el proyecto particularmente interesante porque demuestra que una vieja fotografía nunca se fija completamente: puede ser revisitada, desplazada y hecha para contar una historia diferente.

Lo que finalmente quito de esta edición de los Rencontres d’Arles es esta sucesión de cambios en perspectiva. Mirando un cuerpo, un animal, un trabajador, una madre o una vieja imagen familiar nunca es neutral. Más que nada, los fotógrafos que encontré este año me recordaron que una fotografía no simplemente nos muestra algo: también revela la forma en que decidimos mirarla.

Tímea Urbantsok

Once again this year, Arles was transformed into a vast city devoted to photography. For the 57th edition of the Rencontres d’Arles, I moved through the exhibitions with the sense that, more than the images themselves, it was our way of looking that was being put to the test. From the body to animals, from intimacy to work, from family to forgotten histories, the works I found seemed to raise the same question: what do our images say about us?

I begin with Ming Smith and Lueur nomade, presented at the Église Sainte-Anne. The setting gives the photographs a particular presence: created over several decades, the images enter into dialogue with the historic architecture and seem to hover somewhere between memory, movement and music. Smith photographs cities, encounters, bodies and gestures with a remarkably free approach, in which blur, colour and movement become almost material in themselves. I was drawn to this sense of images that do not attempt to preserve everything. They feel more like memories or fleeting impressions than scenes fixed once and for all.

This attention to the details of everyday life can also be found in the work of Rinko Kawauchi, whose series Aila is presented in Modèle animal. 200 ans de photographie, curated by Nathalie Herschdorfer. Another aspect of her work can be seen in a separate exhibition,From Our Windows, presented with Tokuko Ushioda at Vague as part of Arles Associé. The exhibition explores domestic intimacy, family life and everyday gestures. Belonging to different generations, the two artists observe daily life with great sensitivity. I particularly appreciated their ability to give significance to moments that, taken individually, might seem almost inconsequential.

The gaze becomes far more direct in L’image cannibale, presented at the Chapelle de la Charité. The exhibition approaches photography as a medium that “devours” what it represents. Among the works that struck me most was Mélissa Boucher Morales’s Scrolling [faire défiler] (2024). Using analogue photography, the artist photographs images taken from streaming videos featuring cam girls, post-pornography and feminist pornography. She isolates fragments of bodies and gestures lost within the digital flow, transforming them until they acquire an almost spectral appearance. A reflective pane of glass is then placed over the images, confronting viewers with their own position as voyeurs. I found the installation particularly compelling because it slows down images that would normally be consumed very quickly, forcing us to consider our own way of looking.

At La Mécanique générale, Modèle animal. 200 ans de photographie extends this reflection to the way we look at animals. Rather than following a chronological structure, the exhibition is organised around seven photographic perspectives: the anatomical gaze, which observes and classifies; the performative gaze, which records animal feats; the affective gaze, centred on domestic animals; the fascinated gaze, which celebrates their beauty; the ethical gaze, which makes their exploitation visible; the aesthetic gaze, which explores their forms and visual potential; and finally the viral gaze, which appropriates and circulates images until the boundaries between reality and fiction begin to blur.

What interested me most here is that the exhibition ultimately says as much about us as it does about animals. Whether we photograph an animal to study, love, admire, exploit or protect it reveals our own position in relation to the living world. Two hundred years of photography thus allow us to trace the evolution of our relationship with animals, but also the changing ways in which we position ourselves in relation to them.

I also discovered 5bis, Charlotte Gainsbourg’s exhibition exploring her relationship with her family home on rue de Verneuil in Paris and the legacy left by her father, Serge Gainsbourg. Through photographs, objects and fragments of memory, she constructs an intimate narrative around a place that has become legendary. I was drawn to the deeply personal nature of the project: the house is not simply a setting, but becomes almost a character in its own right, filled with memories and absence.

With Harry Gruyaert’s A Sense of Place [Le sens du lieu], photography returns to the city and to travel. Presented at the Chapelle Saint-Martin du Méjan, the exhibition brings together images taken in cities as varied as New York, Paris, Tokyo, Moscow and Mumbai. Gruyaert does not so much document destinations as construct landscapes out of colour, form and fragments of urban life. Within this former chapel, the contrast between the architecture and the chromatic richness of his photographs makes the experience particularly immersive.

At Ground Control, a former railway site, Vigilance. Le travail sous tension particularly caught my attention. The exhibition brings together photographic archives relating to electricity, industry and, above all, the prevention of workplace accidents. Behind monumental images of electrical infrastructure, workers gradually emerge, along with technical gestures and the invisible dangers associated with their jobs. I found the project particularly interesting because it demonstrates how an apparently documentary photograph can also become a tool for memory and accountability. Things that now seem entirely ordinary to us switching a light on, operating a machine depend on labour and risks that we rarely see.

Finally, at the Fondation Manuel Rivera-Ortiz, Come Together brings together artists exploring different forms of connection: family, solidarity, separation, transmission, encounters and isolation. Among the projects on view, Andi Gáldi Vinkó’s Sorry I Gave Birth I Disappeared But Now I’m Back (2016–2022) particularly resonated with me. Drawing on her own experience of motherhood, the artist photographs bodily transformations, exhaustion, children and the upheavals of everyday life, while questioning the place of a woman artist after giving birth.

I appreciated the way Gáldi Vinkó refuses to present motherhood as either an entirely joyful or an entirely difficult experience. Instead, she reveals its contradictions: love and exhaustion, joy and the loss of freedom, the experience of being a mother and the need to reclaim her place as an artist. It is precisely this honesty that makes the project feel both deeply personal and universal.

I end my visit with Lee Shulman and Omar Victor Diop’s The Anonymous Project – Being There. The artists intervene in American family photographs from the 1950s and 1960s, introducing a Black presence into scenes where history and racial segregation had made such a presence impossible. These apparently ordinary scenes become alternative images, revealing everything that photographs can leave outside the frame. I found the project particularly interesting because it demonstrates that an old photograph is never entirely fixed: it can be revisited, displaced and made to tell a different story.

What I ultimately take away from this edition of the Rencontres d’Arles is this succession of shifts in perspective. Looking at a body, an animal, a worker, a mother or an old family picture is never neutral. More than anything, the photographers I encountered this year reminded me that a photograph does not simply show us something: it also reveals the way we choose to look at it.

Tímea Urbantsok

¿Y si las historias ambientales más poderosas no son sólo sobre lo que estamos perdiendo, sino sobre las personas que encuentran maneras de avanzar?

El 31 de agosto, Vital Impacts abrió aplicaciones para sus 2027 Becas y Mentorías de Fotografía Ambiental, apoyando a fotógrafos de todo el mundo que utilizan narración visual para explorar algunos de los desafíos más urgentes de nuestro planeta y a las personas y comunidades que trabajan todos los días para abordarlos.

Ahora entrando en su cuarto ciclo, el programa proporcionará 50.000 dólares en financiación, orientación y apoyo profesional a narradores visuales cuyo trabajo demuestra el poder de la fotografía para profundizar la comprensión, desafiar las suposiciones e inspirar la acción.

En 2027, Vital Impacts otorgará:

  • Una beca de 20.000 dólaresa un fotógrafo ambiental establecido;
  • Seis $5,000 becasa los fotógrafos emergentes de todo el mundo; y
  • Diez tutoríaspara fotógrafos cuyo trabajo demuestra una promesa excepcional y se beneficiaría de orientaciones adicionales, comunidad y profesionales

Las becas honran los legados de los extraordinarios líderes ambientales cuyas vidas han demostrado que el cambio duradero comienza con curiosidad, valentía y voluntad de ver el mundo de manera diferente: Dra. Jane Goodall, Dra. Sylvia Earle, Hindou Oumarou Ibrahim, Ian Lemaiyan, Chico Mendes, Madonna Thunder Hawk y E. O. Wilson.

Más allá de documentar un problema

La fotografía ambiental a menudo ha pedido al público que mire lo que está desapareciendo. Vital Impacts cree que la fotografía también puede ayudarnos a ver lo que es posible.

El programa busca fotógrafos que están construyendo relaciones a largo plazo con comunidades, documentando soluciones de conservación y medio ambiente, y contando historias que revelan nuevas formas de vivir junto al mundo natural.

“Estos son tiempos extraordinarios, y es fácil llegar a ser abrumado por la magnitud de los desafíos que enfrenta nuestro planeta”, dijo Ami Vitale, fundador de Vital Impacts. “Pero en todas partes que he trabajado, también he encontrado personas que se niegan a renunciar, encontrando maneras para que las comunidades y la naturaleza prosperen juntos. Necesitamos estas historias ahora. La fotografía puede ayudarnos a ver no sólo lo que está en juego, sino lo que es posible”.

Los beneficiarios de becas tendrán hasta el 31 de diciembre de 2027, para desarrollar sus proyectos, con mentoría continua y apoyo de Vital Impacts para ayudar a publicar, amplificar y mostrar su trabajo.

Diez nuevos fotógrafos participarán en un programa intensivo de mentores diseñado para fortalecer su narración, ampliar las redes profesionales y apoyar su desarrollo a largo plazo.

También se invitará a todos los solicitantes a participar en la serie de altavoces en línea Vital Impacts, con fotógrafos, editores, científicos, conservacionistas y otros líderes que trabajan en la intersección de narración y acción ambiental.

Una oportunidad global para los fotógrafos

Las aplicaciones están abiertas a los fotógrafos de todo el mundo. no requerido. Vital Impacts está particularmente interesado en fotógrafos con relaciones comunitarias significativas y un compromiso a largo plazo con las personas e historias que documentan.

Las propuestas pueden presentarse en inglés o en idioma nativo del solicitante. Se proporcionarán servicios de traducción para presentaciones no inglesas para apoyar un proceso de revisión justo y reflexivo.

Esta es una oportunidad para desarrollar historias visuales ambiciosas y profundamente reportadas y para traer imágenes y perspectivas al mundo que de otro modo podrían permanecer inéditas.

What if the most powerful environmental stories are not only about what we are losing, but about the people finding ways forward?

On Aug. 31, Vital Impacts opened applications for its 2027 Environmental Photography Fellowships and Mentorships, supporting photographers around the world who use visual storytelling to explore some of our planet’s most urgent challenges and the people and communities working every day to address them.

Now entering its fourth cycle, the program will provide $50,000 in funding, mentorship, and professional support to visual storytellers whose work demonstrates the power of photography to deepen understanding, challenge assumptions, and inspire action.

In 2027, Vital Impacts will award:

  • One $20,000 fellowshipto an established environmental photographer;
  • Six $5,000 fellowshipsto emerging photographers from around the world; and
  • Ten mentorshipsfor photographers whose work shows exceptional promise and would benefit from additional guidance, community, and professional

The fellowships honor the legacies of extraordinary environmental leaders whose lives have demonstrated that lasting change begins with curiosity, courage, and a willingness to see the world differently: Dr. Jane Goodall, Dr. Sylvia Earle, Hindou Oumarou Ibrahim, Ian Lemaiyan, Chico Mendes, Madonna Thunder Hawk, and E. O. Wilson.

Beyond documenting a problem

Environmental photography has often asked audiences to look at what is disappearing. Vital Impacts believes photography can also help us see what is possible.

The program seeks photographers who are building long-term relationships with communities, documenting conservation and environmental solutions, and telling stories that reveal new ways of living alongside the natural world.

“These are extraordinary times, and it is easy to become overwhelmed by the scale of the challenges facing our planet,” said Ami Vitale, founder of Vital Impacts. “But everywhere I have worked, I have also encountered people who are refusing to give up, finding ways for communities and nature to thrive together. We need these stories now. Photography can help us see not only what is at stake, but what is possible.”

Fellowship recipients will have until December 31, 2027, to develop their projects, with ongoing mentorship and support from Vital Impacts to help publish, amplify, and showcase their work.

Ten additional emerging photographers will participate in an intensive mentorship program designed to strengthen their storytelling, expand professional networks, and support their long-term development.

All applicants will also be invited to participate in the Vital Impacts online speaker series, featuring photographers, editors, scientists, conservationists, and other leaders working at the intersection of storytelling and environmental action.

A global opportunity for photographers

Applications are open to photographers worldwide. Prior publication experience is not required. Vital Impacts is particularly interested in photographers with meaningful community relationships and a long-term commitment to the people and stories they document.

Proposals may be submitted in English or in the applicant’s native language. Translation services will be provided for non-English submissions to support a fair and thoughtful review process.

This is an opportunity to develop ambitious, deeply reported visual stories and to bring images and perspectives to the world that might otherwise remain unseen.

Vital Impacts is a nonprofit organization harnessing the power of storytelling to inspire action for people and the planet. Vital Impacts supports photographers and storytellers through fellowships, mentorships, education, and opportunities to amplify stories that illuminate environmental challenges and the people creating solutions.
